CH2 · UNIT 03 · MODULE 3.2

Meiosis & Mutations

How a germ cell halves its chromosomes to make gametes, why every gamete is different, and how mutations, the ultimate source of new alleles, change DNA. Parts 1 to 3 are meiosis and the genetic variation it creates. Parts 4 and 5 are mutations, from one letter to whole chromosomes.

BEFORE YOU START This module builds on Module 3.1, Cell Division & the Cell Cycle, which sets binary fission, mitosis and meiosis side by side and goes in depth on the two that copy DNA (binary fission and mitosis, with the cell cycle). This module goes inside the one that mixes DNA: meiosis I and II stage by stage, how meiosis makes variation, and mutations.

MODULE 3.2 · PART 1

Reproduction and the job of meiosis

THE QUESTION Why do most organisms bother with sex, and which cells make the gametes?

In this part: asexual vs. sexual reproduction, the trade-offs, where meiosis fits in a life cycle, and the words for describing chromosomes.

START HERE

Two ways to reproduce

Reproduction is a basic property of every living thing. There are two ways to do it, and they differ in how many parents are involved and in how alike the offspring are.

INTERACTIVE · ONE PARENT OR TWO

Asexual vs. sexual reproduction

Tap a button to explore
ASEXUAL REPRODUCTIONOne parent, identical offspringOne parent makes offspring by mitosis (or, in prokaryotes, binary fission). Every offspring has the same DNA as the parent, except for new mutations.
SEXUAL REPRODUCTIONTwo parents, mixed offspringEach parent makes haploid gametes by meiosis, and two gametes fuse at fertilization. Each offspring gets half its chromosomes from each parent, so it is a new mixture, unlike either parent.
WHY IT MATTERSSexual populations grow more slowlyIn an asexual population every offspring can reproduce, so numbers can double every generation. In a sexual population only females produce new offspring, so it takes a pair to make each new individual.
TAP ONEHow many parents?Tap asexual, then sexual, then compare how fast each population grows.
ASEXUALExamplesBacteria and archaea (binary fission), yeast (budding), strawberry plants (runners), hydra (budding), and a few animals such as aphids and whiptail lizards, whose females can produce young without mating.
SEXUALExamplesMost animals and plants, including humans. Most organisms reproduce sexually at least part of the time.
EVEN BACTERIA SHARE DNABacteria and archaea reproduce asexually, but they still have ways to exchange genetic material between individuals, for example conjugation.
KEY TERMS · TAP ONE TO OPEN IT
Asexual reproduction

Reproduction by one parent alone. The offspring are genetically identical to the parent, except for new mutations.

Sexual reproduction

Reproduction in which meiosis makes haploid gametes and two gametes, usually from two parents, fuse at fertilization. Each offspring gets one set of chromosomes from each parent.

TRADE-OFFS

Why bother with sex?

Sexual reproduction costs more, yet most organisms do it at least some of the time. The payoff is genetic variation.

SEXUAL REPRODUCTIONASEXUAL REPRODUCTION
AdvantagesHigh genetic variability · rapid adaptation to new environments and parasites · recombination helps eliminate deleterious mutationsSaves energy · courtship and mates are not needed · faster population growth
DisadvantagesCosts energy · courtship takes time and resources · only females produce new offspring, so growth is slowerLow genetic variability · adapting to a changing environment is difficult · the only way to eliminate deleterious mutations is death
COUNT IT OUTSay every female has 2 offspring. Asexual: 100 females → 200 offspring, all females, all able to reproduce: the population doubles. Sexual: 100 individuals are about 50 females and 50 males → 100 offspring, half of them males: the population only replaces itself. That is the cost of "only females produce new offspring". It comes from needing males, not from meiosis being a slower cell division.
A SHUFFLED DECKMeiosis deals each gamete a random hand of the parents' chromosomes, and fertilization combines two hands. No two offspring get the same cards. Parasites and viruses adapt to the host genotypes that are common, so a population that reshuffles every generation stays a moving target. Part 3 counts the hands: 2ⁿ kinds of gamete, 2²³ ≈ 8 million for one person.
THE KEY DIFFERENCEAsexual offspring are copies, so a whole population can share the same weakness. Sexual reproduction shuffles alleles every generation, so offspring differ, and some may survive a new disease or a new environment. Increased genetic variation is the key consequence of sexual reproduction.
Check yourself: How do these differences affect genetic variation in a population?

Asexual populations get new variation only from mutations, so they have low variation. Sexual populations also recombine and shuffle existing alleles in every generation (Part 3), so they have high variation, which lets them adapt faster to new environments and parasites.

THE LIFE CYCLE

Where meiosis fits

Meiosis happens in only one kind of cell and at one point in the life cycle: germ cells, when they make gametes. Mitosis does everything else.1,2

INTERACTIVE · ONE PAIR OF CHROMOSOMES THROUGH A LIFE

Diploid, haploid, diploid again

Tap a button to explore
MEIOSISGerm cells make gametesDiploid germ cells in the ovaries and testes go through meiosis. Each gamete gets one chromosome of every pair, so it is haploid and carries A or a, never both. The amount of hereditary material is halved.
FERTILIZATIONTwo gametes make a zygoteA haploid egg and a haploid sperm fuse: n + n = 2n. The zygote is diploid again, with one set from each parent. The normal amount of hereditary material is restored.
MITOSISThe zygote builds a bodyThe zygote divides by mitosis into every cell of the body, somatic cells and germ cells alike. All are diploid with the same DNA as the zygote (A and a).
TAP A STEPFollow A and aOne pair of chromosomes: pink from the mother (A), blue from the father (a). Tap each step to see which cells have which.
SOMATIC CELLS2n · the same DNABody cells, made by mitosis. Diploid, with both alleles of every gene (A and a).
GERM CELLS2n · the gamete makersAlso diploid, with the same DNA. Their job: undergo meiosis to make gametes. Only their DNA reaches the next generation.
GAMETESn · one of eachHaploid eggs and sperm, each with one allele of every gene, and genetically different from one another.
Check yourself: What is the end result of meiosis? How many rounds of division, how many cells, what ploidy?

Meiosis ends with 4 haploid daughter cells (gametes in animals), each genetically different. It takes two rounds of cell division (meiosis I and II) after one round of DNA replication. It happens only in diploid germ cells, located in the ovaries and testes in humans.

COMMON MIX-UPMeiosis makes gametes only in animals. That is not true of every eukaryote. In plants and fungi, meiosis makes haploid spores, not gametes. A spore divides by mitosis and grows into a haploid body, and that haploid body makes the gametes, also by mitosis. In seed plants, the pollen grain is that small haploid body: it makes the sperm by mitosis (and the egg is made the same way inside the ovule). Plants switch between a haploid body and a diploid body, the alternation of generations from Module 2.3; pollinators carrying pollen between flowers are in Module 2.1. Either way, meiosis halves the chromosome number (dogs: germ cells 2n = 78, gametes n = 39).
KEY TERMS · TAP ONE TO OPEN IT
Germ cells

The diploid cells that give rise to gametes by meiosis, in the ovaries and testes in humans. (The textbook also counts the gametes themselves as germ cells.)

Gametes

Haploid reproductive cells made by meiosis: eggs and sperm. Each carries one allele of every gene.

Egg

The female gamete: a large haploid cell. In humans it carries 22 autosomes and an X.

Sperm

The male gamete: a small haploid cell with a flagellum. In humans it carries 22 autosomes and either an X or a Y.

Fertilization

The fusion of a haploid egg and a haploid sperm into a diploid zygote. It restores the chromosome number: n + n = 2n.

Zygote

The diploid cell formed at fertilization, the first cell of a new organism. It divides by mitosis to build the body.

THE WORDS

Homologs, chromatids and ploidy

Before following chromosomes through meiosis, get the words straight. Meiosis only works in a cell that has homologous pairs: two of each kind of chromosome, one from each parent.3

INTERACTIVE · ONE HOMOLOGOUS PAIR

Tap a term to see it

Tap the buttons, or Next, to click through all 6
BEFORE SUnreplicated chromosomesEach chromosome is one DNA molecule. The pink one came from the mother and carries allele A; the blue one came from the father and carries a.
AFTER SA replicated chromosomeDNA replication happens before meiosis starts, in S phase. Each chromosome becomes two sister chromatids, identical copies with the same allele (A and A).
NON-SISTER CHROMATIDSOne chromatid from each homologA pink chromatid and a blue chromatid are non-sister chromatids: same genes in the same order, but not identical. Crossing over happens between them.
HOMOLOGOUS CHROMOSOMESThe pairSimilar in size, shape and gene content, with the same genes at the same loci, one inherited from each parent. B and b, or A and a, are different alleles of the same gene.
TETRAD (BIVALENT)The pair joined togetherIn meiosis I the two replicated homologs pair up and lie side by side: four chromatids, a tetrad or bivalent. This is the only time homologs pair.
CENTROMERECount theseOne centromere per chromosome, replicated or not. Count centromeres to count chromosomes; count chromatids to count DNA molecules.
Check yourself: Why does meiosis only occur in cells that have at least 2n DNA content?

Meiosis halves the chromosome number by separating homologous pairs into different cells. Only a cell with two of each chromosome (diploid or more) has pairs to separate, so each gamete still gets one complete set. A haploid cell has no homologs; splitting it in half would leave each daughter cell missing chromosomes.

COMMON MIX-UPSister chromatids are copies of one chromosome (made in S phase). Homologous chromosomes are two chromosomes, one from each parent. Sisters carry the same allele; homologs can carry different alleles (A and a).
KNOW THIS TABLE · DESCRIBING A CELL'S CHROMOSOMES

The vocabulary, in one place

TERMWHAT IT MEANSEXAMPLE
ChromosomeDNA and proteins carrying the cell's hereditary information (genes)Eukaryotes: linear chromosomes; bacteria and archaea: usually one circular one

KEY TERMS · TAP ONE TO OPEN IT
Homologous chromosome

One of a pair of chromosomes similar in size, shape and gene content, one inherited from each parent. They carry the same genes at the same loci, but can carry different alleles.

Locus

The place on a chromosome where a particular gene sits. Homologous chromosomes carry the same genes at the same loci (plural of locus).

Allele

One version of a gene. Different alleles have different DNA sequences. A diploid cell has two alleles of each gene, one on each homolog; a gamete has one.

Sister chromatids

The two copies in a replicated chromosome, made in S phase. They are identical, except for a new mutation or a crossover.

Non-sister chromatids

Chromatids that belong to different homologous chromosomes. Crossing over happens between non-sister chromatids.

Tetrad

A pair of replicated homologous chromosomes joined together in prophase I: four chromatids. Also called a bivalent.

Ploidy

The number of each type of chromosome present: the number of complete sets.

Haploid

Having one of each type of chromosome: one complete set (n).

Diploid

Having two of each type of chromosome (2n), one set from each parent, so chromosomes come in homologous pairs.

Sex chromosome

A chromosome associated with an individual's sex: X and Y in humans (females XX, males XY).

Autosome

Any chromosome that is not a sex chromosome: chromosomes 1 to 22 in humans.

Lock it in · Part 1

  1. Asexual reproduction: one parent, identical offspring, fast growth, low variation. Sexual: two parents, mixed offspring, costly, high variation.
  2. Meiosis happens only in diploid germ cells; it makes 4 haploid gametes. Fertilization (n + n) restores 2n. Mitosis builds the body from the zygote.
  3. Somatic and germ cells are 2n with the same DNA; gametes are n with one allele of each gene.
  4. Sister chromatids = copies of one chromosome. Homologs = a pair, one from each parent, same genes at the same loci. A tetrad (bivalent) = the replicated pair joined in meiosis I.
  5. Meiosis needs homologous pairs to separate, so only a cell with at least two sets can do it.

MODULE 3.2 · PART 2

Meiosis, step by step

THE QUESTION How does one diploid germ cell end up as four haploid gametes, with only one round of DNA replication?

In this part: why meiosis has the same phases as mitosis, twice, every stage of meiosis, the drawings to know, how ploidy and counts change, how meiosis compares with mitosis, and how eggs and sperm differ.

SAME NAMES, TWICE

Phases of meiosis: the same four as mitosis, run twice

If meiosis looks a lot like mitosis, that is because it uses the same phases: prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase. Mitosis goes through them once. Meiosis goes through them twice, meiosis I and then meiosis II, after a single round of DNA replication.1,2

INTERACTIVE · ONE GRID, THREE COLUMNS

Mitosis vs. meiosis I vs. meiosis II, phase by phase

Tap a button to explore
SAME NAMESProphase, metaphase, anaphase, telophaseBoth divisions use the same four phases, with the same basic jobs: condense and build a spindle, line up in the middle, pull apart, then split into two cells.Mitosis runs through them once. Meiosis runs through them twice, so each phase name gets a I or a II. Both start after one interphase, where the DNA is copied once.
MEIOSIS I VS. MITOSISSame phases, different partnersThis is where meiosis is new. In prophase I the homologs pair up and cross over, which never happens in mitosis. In metaphase I they line up in pairs, not single file. In anaphase I the homologs separate while the sister chromatids stay together.Result: 2 haploid cells (n), each chromosome still two sister chromatids.
MEIOSIS II VS. MITOSISMitosis again, with half the chromosomesMeiosis II follows straight on, with no S phase first. Each phase works just like mitosis: line up single file, then the sister chromatids separate.The difference is the starting cell: it is haploid, so the result is 4 haploid cells in all, and crossing over made every one different.
TAP ONERead across a rowEach row is one phase. Tap meiosis I or meiosis II to compare it with mitosis.
COMMON MIX-UPMeiosis does not add new phases. It runs the same four phases twice. What changes is meiosis I: homologs pair, cross over and separate. Meiosis II is basically mitosis in a haploid cell.
Check yourself: Which phase of meiosis looks most like metaphase of mitosis, and why?

Metaphase II. In both, each replicated chromosome lines up single file and the sister chromatids separate next. In metaphase I the homologs line up in pairs instead.

Check yourself: Is there an S phase between meiosis I and meiosis II?

No. The DNA is copied once, before meiosis I. That is why one cell can end up as 4 cells with half the chromosomes.

KEY TERMS · TAP ONE TO OPEN IT
Meiosis

The cell division that turns one diploid germ cell into four haploid gametes: one round of DNA replication, then two divisions, meiosis I and meiosis II. The gametes are genetically different from the parent cell and from each other.

Metaphase I and II

Metaphase I: the bivalents line up across the middle of the cell, homologs facing opposite poles. Metaphase II: in each haploid cell the replicated chromosomes line up one by one, as in mitosis.

THE WHOLE PROCESS

Meiosis, stage by stage

One diploid germ cell, one pair of chromosomes (2n = 2), all the way to four gametes. Watch the counts at the bottom: one round of DNA replication, then two divisions.1,2

INTERACTIVE · 9 STAGES · 2n = 2

From one germ cell to four gametes

Tap the buttons, or Next, to click through all 9
BEFORE MEIOSIS · G1A diploid germ cellOne homologous pair: pink from the mother with allele A, blue from the father with allele a. Each chromosome is one DNA molecule.
BEFORE MEIOSIS · S PHASEDNA replication, onceEvery chromosome is copied into two sister chromatids. This is the only round of DNA replication: there is none between meiosis I and II.
MEIOSIS I · PROPHASE IHomologs pair up and cross overChromosomes condense. The two homologs find each other and lie side by side (synapsis), forming a bivalent (tetrad). This is the only time homologous chromosomes pair.Non-sister chromatids exchange segments at a chiasma (crossing over): here the inner chromatids swap their tips. The nuclear envelope breaks down and the spindle forms.
MEIOSIS I · METAPHASE IPairs line up togetherEach bivalent lines up across the middle, its two homologs facing opposite poles. Spindle fibers from one pole attach to one whole homolog.
MEIOSIS I · ANAPHASE IHomologs separateThe homologs are pulled to opposite poles. The centromeres do not split: sister chromatids stay together. This is what halves the chromosome number.
MEIOSIS I · TELOPHASE ITwo haploid cellsCytokinesis gives two cells, each with one replicated chromosome: haploid (n = 1), even though each chromosome still has 2 DNA molecules. One cell got the A homolog, the other the a homolog.
MEIOSIS II · METAPHASE IILine up one by oneIn each cell the replicated chromosome lines up on its own, as in mitosis. Fibers from both poles attach to its two sister chromatids.
MEIOSIS II · ANAPHASE IISister chromatids separateThe centromeres split and the sister chromatids are pulled apart. Each chromatid is now a chromosome.
MEIOSIS II · TELOPHASE IIFour haploid gametesFour haploid cells, each with one chromosome and one DNA molecule. Two carry A and two carry a, and because of crossing over no two are identical.
MEIOSIS ISeparates homologsProphase I: pairing and crossing over. Metaphase I: pairs line up. Anaphase I: homologs go to opposite poles. Result: 2 haploid cells, chromosomes still replicated. The reductional division.
MEIOSIS IISeparates sister chromatidsLike mitosis, but in haploid cells. Metaphase II: line up one by one. Anaphase II: sisters separate. Result: 4 haploid cells with unreplicated chromosomes. The equational division.
Check yourself: If there are two rounds of cell division, does DNA replication happen twice?

No. DNA is replicated once, in S phase before meiosis I. There is no S phase between meiosis I and meiosis II. That is how 4 cells end up with half the DNA of the parent: one copy, two divisions.

Check yourself: What is the ploidy after meiosis I and after meiosis II, starting from a diploid germ cell?

Haploid after meiosis I (each cell has one of each chromosome, though each is still two sister chromatids) and haploid after meiosis II (one of each chromosome, now one chromatid each).

GO DEEPER · FROM THE TEXTBOOKChromosomes first become visible as long thin threads at the start of prophase I. Even the X and Y pair up, but only at their tips, where their DNA matches, and a chiasma forms there too. Chiasmata form at essentially random positions; humans usually have 50 to 60 per meiosis, and most bivalents have at least one. In prometaphase I the nuclear envelope breaks down and spindle fibers from one pole attach to both sister chromatids of a homolog, which is why sisters travel together in anaphase I.
GO DEEPER · MOLECULAR & CELLULAR BIOLOGY
M&C Module 2.3 · DNA & DNA ReplicationSemiconservative replication →What actually happens to the DNA in S phase, strand by strand.M&C Module 2.3 · DNA & DNA ReplicationLeading and lagging strands →How DNA polymerase copies both strands at a replication fork.
COMMON MIX-UPPloidy drops in meiosis I, not meiosis II. Meiosis I separates homologs (2n → n). Meiosis II separates sister chromatids, which halves the DNA but not the number of chromosome types (n → n).
KEY TERMS · TAP ONE TO OPEN IT
Meiosis

The cell division that turns one diploid germ cell into four haploid gametes: one round of DNA replication, then two divisions, meiosis I and meiosis II. The gametes are genetically different from the parent cell and from each other.

Metaphase I and II

Metaphase I: the bivalents line up across the middle of the cell, homologs facing opposite poles. Metaphase II: in each haploid cell the replicated chromosomes line up one by one, as in mitosis.

Bivalent

The same thing as a tetrad: two replicated homologs paired side by side in meiosis I, held together by chiasmata.

Chiasmata

Plural of chiasma: the X-shaped points where two non-sister chromatids of a bivalent have crossed over. They form in prophase I (1 to 3 per chromosome) and hold the homologs together.

PROPHASE I UP CLOSE

Synapsis, bivalents and chiasmata: prophase I as it really looks

Most diagrams start prophase I with neat X-shaped pairs. Real prophase I starts as a tangle: the chromosomes "first appear as long, thin threads present throughout the nucleus," and the homologs find each other and pair up while they're still long. The tidy shapes only appear at the end.1,2

INTERACTIVE · 5 STAGES · 2n = 4

From tangled threads to bivalents

Tap the buttons, or Next, to click through all 5
EARLY PROPHASE ILong, thin, tangled threadsThe chromosomes start to condense and become visible as long, thin threads all through the nucleus, tangled together. DNA was already copied in S phase, so each thread is two sister chromatids (the two thin lines of one color).The threads are chromatin: DNA wound on proteins, not loose DNA.
SYNAPSISEach chromosome finds its homologEach chromosome pairs with its homolog, the same chromosome from the other parent, and the two zip together along their whole length, still long and wavy. This pairing is synapsis, and it happens only in meiosis.The zipped pair is a bivalent (tetrad): 2 chromosomes, 4 chromatids. Even X and Y pair, but only at their tips.
CROSSING OVERSwapping pieces while zippedWhile the homologs are zipped, two non-sister chromatids (one pink, one blue) break at the same place and rejoin to each other's piece: crossing over. Matching segments are exchanged; usually no DNA is gained or lost.Only 2 of the 4 chromatids swap at each crossover. The spots stay visible as chiasmata (✕). Where they fall is essentially random; most bivalents get at least one (humans: about 50 to 60 per meiosis).
LATE PROPHASE INow it looks like the drawingsThe threads coil up short and thick, and the bivalents finally look like the familiar tidy pictures. The chiasmata hold each pair together until anaphase I.Still count centromeres. 2 bivalents = 4 centromeres = 4 chromosomes, and 8 chromatids. Crossing over moved DNA between chromatids but didn't change any count.
METAPHASE ITop or bottom is randomThe bivalents line up across the middle, one homolog facing each pole. Which one faces up is random, and each pair lines up independently of every other pair.That's independent assortment, the reason behind Mendel's law of independent assortment (Module 3.3).
Check yourself: A bivalent: is it one chromosome or two? Count it.

Two chromosomes. Count centromeres: a bivalent has 2 centromeres, so 2 chromosomes (one homologous pair), with 4 chromatids. A human cell in prophase I has 23 bivalents = 46 chromosomes = 92 chromatids.

COMMON MIX-UPCrossing over and the chiasma aren't two different events. Crossing over is the exchange; a chiasma is the visible X-shaped spot where it happened, which then holds the homologs together. And crossing over is just one source of new combinations: independent assortment (top vs. bottom at metaphase I) is the other one in meiosis.
KEY TERMS · TAP ONE TO OPEN IT
Synapsis

The pairing of homologous chromosomes along their whole length in prophase I, which makes a bivalent. It happens only in meiosis.

Bivalent

The same thing as a tetrad: two replicated homologs paired side by side in meiosis I, held together by chiasmata.

Chiasmata

Plural of chiasma: the X-shaped points where two non-sister chromatids of a bivalent have crossed over. They form in prophase I (1 to 3 per chromosome) and hold the homologs together.

Recombination

New combinations of maternal and paternal alleles on one chromosome, made by crossing over between non-sister chromatids in prophase I.

DRAW IT

The drawings to know

Exams ask you to draw meiosis: before and after DNA replication, at metaphase I and II, and the daughter cells after meiosis I and meiosis II, and to point out sister chromatids and homologs. Here are all six.

INTERACTIVE · FIND THEM

Sister chromatids and homologs

Tap a button to explore
SISTER CHROMATIDSIn metaphase I and metaphase IIEvery chromosome is still replicated at both metaphases, so sister chromatids are there both times. They only separate in anaphase II.
HOMOLOGOUS CHROMOSOMESIn metaphase I onlyAt metaphase I the homologs sit side by side as a pair. After anaphase I they are in different cells, so a metaphase II cell has no homologs: it is haploid.
TAP ONESix drawings, one cell2n = 2: pink from the mother, blue from the father. Tap to find the sister chromatids, then the homologs.
DRAWING TIPSUse two colors, one for maternal and one for paternal chromosomes, as in class. Draw the centromere as a dot. At metaphase I draw the pair side by side across the middle line; at metaphase II draw each chromosome on the line.
Check yourself: A diploid cell with 2n = 4 is in metaphase II. How many chromosomes are in that cell, and are there any homologs?

2 chromosomes (each two sister chromatids), no homologs: they went to different cells in anaphase I. The cell is haploid, n = 2.

COUNT IT

Ploidy and counts, before, during and after

The same counting rules as mitosis: chromosomes = centromeres, DNA molecules = chromatids. What changes in meiosis is the ploidy.

After S (G2)Diploid2 · 446 · 92
Metaphase IDiploid2 · 4 (1 bivalent)46 · 92 (23 bivalents)
After meiosis I (each cell)Haploid1 · 223 · 46
Metaphase II (each cell)Haploid1 · 223 · 46
After meiosis II (each gamete)Haploid1 · 123 · 23
Zygote (egg + sperm)Diploid2 · 246 · 46
Check yourself: A human cell at the end of prophase I: how many chromatids, centromeres and bivalents?

92 chromatids, 46 centromeres (46 chromosomes) and 23 bivalents (one per homologous pair).

Check yourself: A horse germ cell has 2n = 64. How many chromosomes and DNA molecules does each gamete have?

32 chromosomes and 32 DNA molecules. Meiosis halves the chromosome number (64 → 32) and, after two divisions from one replication, each gamete has one DNA molecule per chromosome.

LARGE NUMBERSThe logic never changes with the number. Halve the chromosomes in meiosis I. Halve the DNA again in meiosis II. Replication only happens before meiosis I.
Check yourself: Scarlet dragonflies have 2n = 50. A germ cell in the ovary goes through meiosis. How many chromatids are in each cell at metaphase I? At metaphase II? How many chromosomes in each egg?

100, 50, 25. Metaphase I: 50 replicated chromosomes × 2 = 100 chromatids. Meiosis I halves the number of chromosomes, so at metaphase II each cell has 25 replicated chromosomes × 2 = 50 chromatids. Anaphase II splits the sisters: each egg has 25 chromosomes (n).

KEY TERMS · TAP ONE TO OPEN IT
Haploid number

n: the number of different types of chromosomes in a cell. Humans: n = 23.

Diploid number

2n: the number of chromosomes in a diploid cell. Humans: 2n = 46.

COMPARE

Meiosis vs. mitosis

Meiosis II looks like mitosis. The big differences are all in meiosis I: homologs pair, cross over and separate.1

INTERACTIVE · THREE METAPHASES

How the chromosomes line up

Tap a button to explore
MITOSISSingle file, each pole grabs a sisterIn a diploid cell, each replicated chromosome lines up on its own. Homologs ignore each other.Fibers from both poles attach to every chromosome, one to each sister chromatid. So in anaphase the sisters separate.
MEIOSIS IIn pairs, each pole grabs a whole homologHomologs line up as a pair, side by side across the middle.All the fibers from one pole attach to one homolog (both its sisters), and the other pole takes the other homolog. So in anaphase I the homologs separate while the sisters stay together.
MEIOSIS IISingle file again, each pole grabs a sisterLike mitosis, but the cell is haploid: one of each kind of chromosome.Each chromosome is attached to both poles, one sister to each. So in anaphase II the sisters separate.
TAP ONESame cell, three metaphasesCompare how the chromosomes line up, which chromatids each pole grabs (gold fibers from the left pole, cyan from the right), and what separates next.
MITOSISMEIOSIS
FunctionGrowth, development and repair; asexual reproduction in single-celled eukaryotesSexual reproduction: gametes (and spores)
WhereSomatic cellsOnly germ cells
Rounds of DNA replication11
Cell divisions12
Daughter cells24
Chromosome numberSame as parent (2n → 2n)Half (2n → n)
DNA of daughtersIdentical to parentDifferent from parent and each other
Homologs pair? Cross over?NoYes, in meiosis I only
Homologs separate?NoYes, in meiosis I
Sister chromatids separate?YesYes, in meiosis II
Check yourself: How are mitosis and meiosis similar?

Both happen only in eukaryotes, both follow a single round of DNA replication, both use a spindle to pull chromosomes apart, and both separate sister chromatids at some point (mitosis in anaphase, meiosis in anaphase II). Meiosis II works almost exactly like mitosis.

COMMON MIX-UPMitosis = 2 identical diploid cells (somatic cells). Meiosis = 4 different haploid gametes (germ cells only). Only meiosis pairs up homologs.
WHERE MEIOSIS CAME FROMMitosis happens in all eukaryotes; meiosis in most. Because meiosis II works so much like mitosis, and its steps are the same in every eukaryote, meiosis probably evolved from mitosis in the common ancestor of all eukaryotes.
EGGS VS. SPERM

Same meiosis, different cytoplasm

Meiosis shares out the chromosomes the same way in both sexes, but in animals the cytoplasm divides very differently.1

INTERACTIVE · ONE GERM CELL EACH

How many gametes come out?

Tap a button to explore
FEMALE1 egg and 3 polar bodiesBoth meiotic divisions split the cytoplasm very unequally. One cell keeps nearly all of it and becomes the large egg; the other three, the polar bodies, get very little and do not become eggs.
MALE4 spermThe cytoplasm divides about equally, and all four cells become sperm. While a sperm develops it loses most of its cytoplasm: little more than a nucleus in a head, with a flagellum to swim.
TAP ONEFour haploid cells either wayIn both sexes meiosis makes four haploid cells. Tap to see what becomes of them.
HUMAN GAMETES23 chromosomes eachOne of each of the 22 autosomes, plus an X (every egg) or an X or a Y (each sperm). Meiosis happens in the ovaries and testes.
THE ZYGOTE46: one set from eachFertilization restores the diploid number, so offspring have the same number of chromosomes as each parent.
THE CHROMOSOME THEORY OF INHERITANCEFollowing chromosomes through meiosis and fertilization showed that chromosomes carry the hereditary material from parent to offspring. The idea is credited to Walter Sutton and Theodor Boveri, building on work by Nettie Stevens, Edmund Wilson and others.
KEY TERMS · TAP ONE TO OPEN IT
Polar body

A small cell made by the unequal division of the cytoplasm in female meiosis. It gets very little cytoplasm and does not become an egg.

Egg

The female gamete: a large haploid cell. In humans it carries 22 autosomes and an X.

Sperm

The male gamete: a small haploid cell with a flagellum. In humans it carries 22 autosomes and either an X or a Y.

Lock it in · Part 2

  1. Meiosis uses the same four phases as mitosis (prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase), run twice: meiosis I, then meiosis II.
  2. One DNA replication (S phase), then two divisions. No replication between meiosis I and II.
  3. Meiosis I: prophase I (homologs pair into bivalents, crossing over), metaphase I (pairs line up), anaphase I (homologs separate). 2n → n.
  4. Meiosis II: metaphase II (line up one by one), anaphase II (sister chromatids separate). n → n, like mitosis.
  5. Result: 4 haploid gametes, genetically different. Human: 46 → 23 chromosomes per gamete.
  6. Sister chromatids are present at metaphase I and II; homologs are together only at metaphase I.
  7. Females: 1 egg + 3 polar bodies (unequal cytoplasm). Males: 4 sperm.

MODULE 3.2 · PART 3

Where genetic variation comes from

THE QUESTION Two siblings get their chromosomes from the same two parents. Why aren't they identical?

In this part: why variation matters, then its three sources: crossing over, independent assortment and random fertilization.

WHY IT MATTERS

Three ways meiosis and fertilization make variation

Genetic variation, the genetic differences among individuals in a population, is critical to a species' long-term survival: a species can only adapt to new or changing environments if it has variation. Darwin saw it in 1859: individual differences are what natural selection works on.1,2

VARIATION #1Crossing overIn prophase I, maternal and paternal chromosomes recombine: non-sister chromatids swap segments, making new combinations of alleles on one chromosome.
VARIATION #2Independent assortmentIn metaphase I, each homologous pair lines up independently, so each gamete gets a random mix of maternal and paternal chromosomes: 2ⁿ combinations.
VARIATION #3Random fertilizationAny egg can meet any sperm, so the combinations of the two parents multiply: 2ⁿ × 2ⁿ.
A CATCHThese three only shuffle alleles that already exist. They increase variation only if the maternal and paternal alleles differ, and individuals differ. Those differences come from mutation (Parts 4 and 5), the ultimate source of new variation.
VARIATION #1

Crossing over and recombination

Crossing over happens in prophase I, while the homologs are paired as a bivalent. Usually 1 to 3 chiasmata form per chromosome.3,2

INTERACTIVE · TWO GENES ON ONE CHROMOSOME

How a chiasma makes new combinations

Tap the buttons, or Next, to click through all 4
PROPHASE IThe homologs pair upThe mother's chromosome carries A and D; the father's carries a and d. Each is two sister chromatids.
A CHIASMA FORMSNon-sister chromatids crossTwo non-sister chromatids, one pink and one blue, break at the same place. The chiasma also holds the homologs together until anaphase I.
THEY SWAPMatching segments are exchangedThe broken ends rejoin the other chromatid. The exchange is precise: the same genes, in the same order, no DNA gained or lost. Only the alleles below the break are swapped.
THE RESULTRecombinant chromatidsTwo chromatids keep the parental combinations (A D and a d). Two are recombinant (A d and a D): combinations that neither parent's chromosome had. Each goes to a different gamete.
Check yourself: How might two sister chromatids acquire different alleles of the same gene?

Two ways. A mutation during DNA replication in S phase can change one copy but not the other. Or crossing over can swap a segment of one sister with a non-sister chromatid: after the swap above, the pink chromosome's two sisters carry D and d.

Check yourself: How might two non-sister chromatids of the same homologous pair acquire different alleles?

They come from different parents, so they can carry different alleles from the start (A on the mother's, a on the father's). Mutations in either parent's line made those differences; crossing over then reshuffles them.

COMMON MIX-UPCrossing over is between non-sister chromatids of homologs. Swapping between sisters would change nothing, since they are copies.
KEY TERMS · TAP ONE TO OPEN IT
Chiasmata

Plural of chiasma: the X-shaped points where two non-sister chromatids of a bivalent have crossed over. They form in prophase I (1 to 3 per chromosome) and hold the homologs together.

Recombination

New combinations of maternal and paternal alleles on one chromosome, made by crossing over between non-sister chromatids in prophase I.

VARIATION #2

Independent assortment

At metaphase I, each pair lines up on its own, maternal homolog facing one pole or the other at random. With n pairs there are 2ⁿ combinations. One human can make gametes with 2²³, about 8 million, different combinations of chromosomes.3,2

INTERACTIVE · 2n = 4

Two pairs, two ways to line up

Tap a button to explore
WAY 1Both maternal homologs face one polePink A and pink B go one way, blue a and blue b the other. Gametes: AB and ab.
WAY 2The short pair is flippedPink A goes with blue b, blue a with pink B. Gametes: Ab and aB.
ALL FOUR2² = 4 kinds of gameteTwo pairs, each with 2 orientations: 2 × 2 = 4 combinations. Each orientation is equally likely in every germ cell.
TAP ONEWhat assorts independently?The homologous pairs: how one pair lines up has no effect on how the other lines up.
Check yourself: A germ cell with 2n = 4 undergoes meiosis. How many unique gametes can result, assuming no mutations?

n = 2, so 2² = 4 kinds: AB, Ab, aB, ab. (One germ cell makes 4 gametes using one orientation, two kinds; across many germ cells all 4 kinds appear. Crossing over adds even more.)

THE FORMULA2ⁿ, where n is the haploid number. Humans: n = 23, 2²³ = 8,388,608, about 8 million. This ignores crossing over.
Check yourself: Salamander species A has 2n = 60 and species B has 2n = 98. With no crossing over, which species' offspring will vary more?

Species B. More homologous pairs means more ways to line up in metaphase I: 2⁴⁹ kinds of gametes for B vs. 2³⁰ for A, and random fertilization multiplies that again.

KEY TERMS · TAP ONE TO OPEN IT
Independent assortment

Each homologous pair lines up at metaphase I independently of the others, so each gamete gets a random mix of maternal and paternal chromosomes: 2ⁿ combinations.

VARIATION #3

Random fertilization

Any of a mother's eggs can meet any of a father's sperm. For humans, one couple can make 2²³ × 2²³, about 70 trillion, unique zygotes, and that is without the extra variety from crossing over.2

GRID · TWO PARENTS WITH 2n = 4

Every egg × every sperm

Check yourself: What are the 3 key places genetic variation increases, and how much does each add?

1. Crossing over in prophase I: 1 to 3 chiasmata per chromosome, making new allele combinations on each chromosome (a huge, uncounted number). 2. Independent assortment in metaphase I: 2ⁿ combinations per parent, about 8 million in humans. 3. Random fertilization: 2ⁿ × 2ⁿ, about 70 trillion per human couple, before counting crossing over.

WHAT THE ZYGOTE GETSOne set from the egg, one from the sperm: each pair has one maternal and one paternal homolog, whose alleles can match (B B) or differ (B b).
KEY TERMS · TAP ONE TO OPEN IT
Sexual reproduction

Reproduction in which meiosis makes haploid gametes and two gametes, usually from two parents, fuse at fertilization. Each offspring gets one set of chromosomes from each parent.

Lock it in · Part 3

  1. Genetic variation lets a species adapt; sexual reproduction increases it in three places.
  2. Crossing over (prophase I): non-sister chromatids exchange segments at chiasmata, making recombinant chromosomes.
  3. Independent assortment (metaphase I): pairs orient at random, 2ⁿ combinations; 2²³ ≈ 8 million in humans.
  4. Random fertilization: 2ⁿ × 2ⁿ, about 70 trillion zygotes per human couple.
  5. All three only shuffle existing alleles. New alleles come from mutation.

MODULE 3.2 · PART 4

Point mutations

THE QUESTION Every allele began as a mutation. What kinds of small changes can happen to DNA, and what do they do to a protein?

In this part: what a mutation is and its effects, how a copying error becomes a mutation and how often it happens, substitutions, indels and frameshifts, coding vs. noncoding DNA, and how genotype leads to phenotype.

START HERE

What is a mutation?

A mutation is any heritable change in the genetic material: it is stable and is passed on through cell division (meiosis, mitosis or binary fission). Mutation is the ultimate source of genetic variation: every allele began as one.1,2

INTERACTIVE · WHERE IT LANDS DECIDES ITS EFFECT

Neutral, deleterious or beneficial

Tap a button to explore
NEUTRALNo effect on fitnessMost mutations in noncoding DNA are neutral, and so are synonymous mutations. Neutral is the most common kind.
DELETERIOUSLowers fitnessMost missense, nonsense and frameshift mutations are deleterious: they change or break a protein.
BENEFICIALRaises fitnessFew mutations, coding or noncoding, are beneficial (advantageous). Example: mutations in an enhancer that keep the lactase gene on in adults, so they can digest milk.
TAP ONEThree possible effectsWhether a mutation helps or harms depends on where it lands, and on the environment.
WHENDuring DNA replication, mostlyBy chance, as copying errors during DNA replication, and during mitosis, meiosis or binary fission. Mutagens (such as UV light, X-rays and chemicals in tobacco smoke) raise the rate.
WHEREIn the DNA of any cellIn eukaryotes, mostly in the nuclear DNA in the nucleus (also in the small circles of mitochondrial and chloroplast DNA, which came from bacteria by endosymbiosis: Module 2.2), in any cell of the body.
HOW OFTENRare per letter, common per genomeAbout 1 in 10 billion nucleotides per replication, but a human zygote carries about 60 new ones.
GO DEEPER · MOLECULAR & CELLULAR BIOLOGY
M&C Module 2.5 · Mutation & DNA RepairHow DNA gets damaged →Mutagens: what UV light, X-rays and chemicals do to DNA.M&C Module 2.5 · Mutation & DNA RepairFour ways to fix DNA →The repair systems that keep the mutation rate low.
KEY TERMS · TAP ONE TO OPEN IT
Neutral mutation

A change in coding or noncoding DNA that has no effect on an organism's fitness. The most common kind.

Deleterious mutation

A change in coding or noncoding DNA that has a negative effect on an organism's fitness.

Advantageous mutation

A change in coding or noncoding DNA that has a positive effect on an organism's fitness. Same as beneficial.

Beneficial mutation

A change in coding or noncoding DNA that has a positive effect on an organism's fitness. Same as advantageous.

HOW IT HAPPENS

How a copying error becomes a mutation, and how often

Most mistakes in DNA replication are fixed right away: DNA polymerase proofreads, and repair enzymes catch most of the rest. A fixed mistake is not a mutation. A mutation is a mistake that escapes repair and is then copied.1

INTERACTIVE · 4 STEPS

From a mismatch to a mutation

Tap the buttons, or Next, to click through all 4
THE ORIGINALA T-A base pairA matches T and G matches C. Watch the highlighted T-A pair.
THE MISTAKEA G across from the TDuring replication, DNA polymerase puts a G across from the T. If proofreading and repair miss it, the new DNA has a T-G mismatch.
THE NEXT REPLICATIONEach strand becomes a templateThe T strand is copied into a normal T-A pair. The G strand is copied into a C-G pair.
PERMANENTA substitutionThe C-G pair is perfectly matched, so nothing looks wrong and it is copied faithfully from then on: T-A has been replaced by C-G, a substitution, a point mutation. A variant like this that becomes common in a population is a single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP).
PER NUCLEOTIDEVery rareOnly about 1 nucleotide in every 10 billion is substituted per replication and slips past proofreading and repair. The rate differs about tenfold among organisms; per nucleotide it is highest in bacteria and lowest in humans.
PER GENOMECommonHumans still get the most new mutations per genome per generation, because the genome is large and many cell divisions happen in a lifetime: about 30 new substitutions per genome, about 60 per diploid zygote.
FROM WHICH PARENTMostly the fatherAbout 80% of a zygote's new mutations come from the father: by age 30, the cells that make sperm have gone through about 400 rounds of replication, versus about 30 for eggs, and the number rises with the father's age.
WHICH CELLSSomatic more than germIn mammals the rate per nucleotide is almost 100 times higher in somatic cells than in germ cells, because germ cells repair DNA more efficiently. Some sites, called hotspots, mutate far more often than average.
GO DEEPER · MOLECULAR & CELLULAR BIOLOGY
M&C Module 2.5 · Mutation & DNA RepairThe life of a mistake →The same story in detail: from a copying error to a permanent change.M&C Module 2.5 · Mutation & DNA RepairProofreading and mismatch repair →How the cell catches most mistakes before they become mutations.M&C Module 2.3 · DNA & DNA ReplicationBase pairing →Why A pairs with T and G with C, so a mismatch stands out.
SUBSTITUTIONS

One letter swapped: synonymous, missense, nonsense

A substitution replaces one nucleotide with another. In a coding region, what it does depends on how the mRNA codon changes. 64 codons code for 20 amino acids and 3 stops, so most amino acids have several codons (you don't need to memorize the code).3,1,2

INTERACTIVE · ONE CODON, THREE SUBSTITUTIONS

Identify the mutation type

Tap the buttons, or Next, to click through all 4
THE ORIGINALTTA → UUA → leucineThe coding strand reads TTA, the template strand AAT, so the mRNA codon is UUA, which codes for leucine.
MISSENSE (NONSYNONYMOUS)UUA → GUA: valineA different amino acid. Missense and nonsynonymous mean the same thing. The protein may work worse, or not at all, depending on the change. (The sickle-cell allele is a missense mutation: glutamic acid to valine.)
NONSENSEUUA → UAA: STOPAn early stop codon: translation ends early and the protein is cut short, so it is nearly always nonfunctional. A nonsense mutation is not counted as missense or nonsynonymous.
SYNONYMOUSUUA → CUA: still leucineThe same amino acid, so the protein does not change and the phenotype does not change. Synonymous codons usually differ at the third position, though here it is the first. The textbook's example is in beta-globin: GAG → GAA, both glutamic acid.
Check yourself: Why do synonymous mutations not affect the phenotype?

The new codon codes for the same amino acid, so the protein's amino acid sequence, its folding and its function are unchanged. Nothing about the organism changes.

Check yourself: How can you tell a missense mutation from a nonsense mutation?

Translate the new codon. A different amino acid = missense (nonsynonymous). A stop codon = nonsense.

COMMON MIX-UPSynonymous, missense (nonsynonymous) and nonsense apply only to coding regions and only to substitutions. An indel is never called missense or nonsense.
GO DEEPER · MOLECULAR & CELLULAR BIOLOGY
M&C Module 2.4 · Transcription & TranslationReading a gene: the template strand →Why the coding strand and the mRNA read the same, and the template is the complement.M&C Module 2.4 · Transcription & TranslationThree letters per amino acid →Codons and the genetic code, and why several codons can mean the same amino acid.M&C Module 2.5 · Mutation & DNA RepairThe mutation lab →Try point mutations on a real gene and watch the mRNA and protein change.
Check yourself: Part of the leptin gene's DNA template strand reads TACGGCAGCTAAGCCCATGCG, giving mRNA AUGCCGUCGAUUCGGGUACGC. At position 9 the template C becomes A. Is this both a point mutation and a synonymous mutation?

True. One base changed, so it is a point mutation. Template C → A makes the mRNA G → U at position 9, so codon 3 (positions 7 to 9) goes from UCG to UCU. Both code for serine, so the protein is the same: synonymous. (Read codons in threes from the start, AUG.)

Check yourself: True or false: a substitution that creates an early stop codon is a missense (nonsynonymous) mutation. And: an indel that creates an early stop codon is NOT called a nonsense mutation.

False, then true. A substitution that makes an early stop is a nonsense mutation. An indel that leads to an early stop is still classed as an indel (a frameshift if it is not a multiple of 3), not nonsense.

KEY TERMS · TAP ONE TO OPEN IT
Substitution

Replacement of one nucleotide with another, in coding or noncoding DNA. A type of point mutation.

Synonymous mutation

Coding regions only: a substitution that gives an mRNA codon for the same amino acid. The protein does not change.

Missense mutation

Coding regions only: a substitution that gives an mRNA codon for a different amino acid. Means the same as nonsynonymous.

Nonsynonymous mutation

Coding regions only: a substitution that gives an mRNA codon for a different amino acid. Means the same as missense.

Nonsense mutation

Coding regions only: a substitution (not an indel) that gives an early stop codon in the mRNA. Not counted as missense or nonsynonymous.

INDELS

Letters added or lost: indels and frameshifts

An indel is an insertion or deletion of one or more base pairs. The name covers both because, comparing two sequences, a gap in one could be an insertion in the other or a deletion in the first. Unlike a substitution, an indel changes the length of the DNA.3,1,2

INTERACTIVE · READ IT IN THREES

What a frameshift does

Tap the buttons, or Next, to click through all 4
THE READING FRAMEThree letters at a timeA ribosome reads mRNA in codons of three, starting from the start codon, just as you read this sentence in three-letter words.
INSERT 1 · FRAMESHIFTEverything after it changesOne extra letter shifts the frame: every word after it is gibberish. In DNA, every codon downstream codes for a different amino acid, often hitting an early stop.
DELETE 1 · FRAMESHIFTSame problemLosing one letter (or 2, 4, 5...) shifts the frame the other way. Any indel that is not a multiple of 3 is a frameshift.
INSERT 3 · IN FRAMEOne extra wordThree letters add exactly one codon: one extra amino acid (or one fewer for a deletion), and the rest of the protein is unchanged.
Check yourself: How does a frameshift mutation differ from an indel of 3 nucleotides? (Process and result.)

Process: a frameshift is an indel of a number of bases that is not a multiple of 3 (such as 1 or 2); a 3-nucleotide indel adds or removes exactly one codon. Result: a frameshift changes every codon after it, usually giving a nonfunctional protein; a 3-nucleotide indel adds or removes one amino acid and leaves the rest unchanged.

Check yourself: Which is more likely to be deleterious: a frameshift, or an indel of 3 nucleotides?

The frameshift. It scrambles the whole protein after the indel; an in-frame indel changes only one amino acid.

COMMON MIX-UPA frameshift that happens to create an early stop is still called a frameshift, not nonsense. An indel of 3 is not missense.
A REAL 3-BASE DELETION · CYSTIC FIBROSISThe most common cystic fibrosis mutation, ΔF508, deletes exactly one codon from the CFTR gene, so the protein loses one amino acid: the phenylalanine at position 508. CFTR is a chloride channel; without that one amino acid it folds wrongly and is destroyed before it reaches the membrane, so thick, sticky mucus builds up in the lungs. With good care, life expectancy is now about 45 years, and a three-drug combination can improve the mutant protein's function by 10% to 15%.
GO DEEPER · MOLECULAR & CELLULAR BIOLOGY
M&C Module 2.5 · Mutation & DNA RepairInsertions, deletions and frameshifts →More examples, on the same gene as the mutation lab.M&C Module 2.4 · Transcription & TranslationTranslation, start to finish →How the ribosome sets the reading frame at the start codon and reads codon by codon.
KEY TERMS · TAP ONE TO OPEN IT
Indel (insertion/deletion)

Insertion or deletion of one or more base pairs, in coding or noncoding DNA. A type of point mutation.

Frameshift mutation

Coding regions only: an indel of a number of bases that is not a multiple of 3, which shifts the mRNA's reading frame from that point on. Not counted as missense, even if it makes an early stop.

CODING VS. NONCODING

Which types need a coding region?

Most of the human genome does not code for protein: about 2.5% does, and more than 90% of the nucleotides seem free to vary without harm. That is why each of us can carry about 60 new mutations and be fine. A mutation in noncoding DNA usually has no effect, but some noncoding DNA regulates genes, and a mutation there can matter.1,3

MUTATION TYPECODING ONLY?WHAT IT IS
Point mutationNo: coding or noncodingA small change of one or a few nucleotides at one location: substitutions and indels
SubstitutionNo: coding or noncodingOne nucleotide replaced by another
IndelNo: coding or noncodingOne or more base pairs inserted or deleted
SynonymousYesA substitution giving a codon for the same amino acid
Missense = nonsynonymousYesA substitution giving a codon for a different amino acid
NonsenseYesA substitution giving an early stop codon
FrameshiftYesAn indel not a multiple of 3, shifting the reading frame
Check yourself: What is the difference between the effects of mutations in coding vs. noncoding regions?

In a coding region a mutation can change the protein in a predictable way (synonymous: no change; missense: one amino acid; nonsense: cut short; frameshift: scrambled). In noncoding DNA most mutations have no effect, because most noncoding DNA has no known function. But mutations in regulatory sequences can change how much of a protein is made, and some of these are evolutionarily important.

COMMON MIX-UPThe course's definition of point mutation is broader than the textbook's. Here: one or a few nucleotides, so substitutions and indels are both point mutations. The textbook limits point mutations to single-nucleotide substitutions. Use the course's definition.

A NOTE ON WORDINGThe Molecular & Cellular mutation module uses the textbook's narrower meaning of point mutation (one base pair) and the word "silent" for synonymous. Same ideas; for this module, use the broader definition above.
KEY TERMS · TAP ONE TO OPEN IT
Point mutation

A small change of one or a few nucleotides at one place in the genome, in coding or noncoding DNA. Substitutions and indels are point mutations. (The textbook uses a narrower definition: a change in a single nucleotide.)

GENOTYPE TO PHENOTYPE

From a change in DNA to a change in the organism

Genetic variation matters for evolution because it creates heritable differences in phenotype. But many mutations change no trait at all, and the ones that do can have different effects depending on the rest of the genotype and on the environment.1,2

GENOTYPEWhat alleles it carriesThe genetic makeup of a cell or organism. Any two people differ at about 3 million nucleotide sites, about one in a thousand.
ALLELESDifferent DNA sequencesThe different forms of a gene are called alleles, and they correspond to different DNA sequences, polymorphisms, in the gene. A polymorphism is a variant shared by many individuals.
PHENOTYPEWhat you can observeTraits such as height, eye color, lactose intolerance or color blindness. A phenotype results from the genotype interacting with the environment.
EXAMPLE · ONE GENE, THREE ALLELES

Hemoglobin's beta-globin gene

Tap a button to explore
ALLELE AThe most commonGAG codes for glutamic acid. People with two copies (homozygous AA) have typical hemoglobin.
ALLELE SOne base changed: a missense mutationGTG codes for valine. One amino acid changes the way the protein folds and works: SS causes sickle-cell anemia. AS (heterozygous) gives only a mild anemia, and where malaria is common it protects against malaria, so there it is beneficial. Where there is no malaria, it is harmful.
ALLELE CAnother missense mutationAAG codes for lysine. AC gives partial protection against malaria; CC gives more protection and only a very mild anemia.
TAP AN ALLELEHow a DNA change reaches the phenotypeDNA sequence → mRNA codon → amino acid sequence → how the protein folds → how it works → the trait. You don't need to memorize these alleles: they show the principle.
TWO PRINCIPLES1. A mutation's effect can depend on whether it is homozygous or heterozygous (S is harmful as SS, beneficial as AS in malaria regions). 2. It can depend on the environment (AS helps only where there is malaria). So "harmful, neutral or beneficial" is often an oversimplification.
HARMFULExampleHuntington's disease: the HTT gene normally has 6 to 35 repeats of the codon CAG; mutant forms with 36 to 250 cause nerve cells to degenerate.
NEUTRALExampleWhether you taste the bitter chemical phenylthiocarbamide depends largely on alleles of a taste receptor gene; either way survival and reproduction are unaffected.
BENEFICIALExampleLactase persistence: enhancer mutations that keep lactase on in adults, common where dairy farming began. About 35% of people worldwide can digest milk as adults; the alleles arose about 11,000 years ago, around when cattle were domesticated.
NONCODING MATTERS TOOThe textbook plays down mutations outside genes. But some noncoding mutations change how genes are regulated, like the lactase enhancer, and can have evolutionarily important effects on the phenotype.
GO DEEPER · MOLECULAR & CELLULAR BIOLOGY
M&C Module 2.5 · Mutation & DNA RepairSickle cell and cystic fibrosis →The S allele and a 3-base deletion, traced from DNA to protein to disease.
KEY TERMS · TAP ONE TO OPEN IT
Genotype

The genetic makeup of a cell or organism: which alleles it carries.

Phenotype

An organism's observable characteristics or traits (appearance, physiology, behavior). It results from the genotype interacting with the environment.

Polymorphism

A genetic difference among individuals that is present in many individuals of a population. Alleles correspond to different DNA sequences, polymorphisms, in a gene.

Homozygous

Having two copies of the same allele of a gene (for example AA).

Heterozygous

Having two different alleles of a gene (for example AS).

Lock it in · Part 4

  1. A mutation is a heritable change in DNA, the ultimate source of genetic variation. It happens by chance, mostly during DNA replication.
  2. Most mutations are neutral; most missense, nonsense and frameshift mutations are deleterious; a few are beneficial.
  3. Substitution (one base swapped): synonymous (same amino acid), missense = nonsynonymous (different amino acid), nonsense (early stop).
  4. Indel (bases added or lost): not a multiple of 3 = frameshift; a multiple of 3 adds or removes whole amino acids.
  5. Synonymous, missense, nonsense and frameshift happen only in coding regions; substitutions and indels can happen anywhere.
  6. A mismatch that escapes repair becomes permanent at the next replication. Mutations are rare per nucleotide but common per genome; most new ones come from the father.
  7. Genotype + environment → phenotype. Alleles are different DNA sequences (polymorphisms). Effects can depend on homozygous vs. heterozygous and on the environment.

MODULE 3.2 · PART 5

Chromosomal mutations, and where mutations come from

THE QUESTION What happens when whole chunks of chromosomes, or whole chromosomes, go wrong, and do mutations happen because an organism needs them?

In this part: chromosomal mutations, nondisjunction, karyotypes, the Lederbergs' experiment, germ-line vs. somatic, the big ideas, and every type sorted.

BIG CHANGES

Chromosomal mutations

Some mutations affect large regions: hundreds of thousands to millions of nucleotides, often big enough to see under a microscope. They change how many copies of genes there are, or where the genes sit.1,2

INTERACTIVE · FOUR KINDS

Duplication, deletion, inversion, translocation

Tap the buttons, or Next, to click through all 4
GENE DUPLICATIONAn extra copyA segment appears twice. A duplicated gene's extra copy is free to collect mutations, and it often ends up coding for a protein with a new function. That is how gene families arise.
GENE DELETIONA missing pieceA chromosome loses a segment and the genes in it. Usually more harmful than a duplication of the same region.
INVERSIONFlipped aroundBoth DNA strands break in two places and the piece reattaches in reverse orientation, changing the order of genes. If whole genes and their regulatory sequences survive the breaks, it may have no effect.
RECIPROCAL TRANSLOCATIONTwo chromosomes swapTwo non-homologous chromosomes break (both strands), and each broken piece attaches to the other chromosome. It may or may not have effects, depending on where the breaks are and whether regulatory regions are hit.
Check yourself: How do point mutations differ from chromosomal-scale mutations?

Point mutations change one or a few nucleotides at one place (substitutions, indels). Chromosomal mutations change large segments or whole chromosomes: duplications, deletions, inversions, translocations, and changes in chromosome number (aneuploidy, polyploidy).

Check yourself: How does a reciprocal translocation differ from crossing over in meiosis I?

Crossing over is a normal part of meiosis between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes: they swap matching segments precisely, so every gene stays at its locus and only alleles are reshuffled. A reciprocal translocation is a mutation between non-homologous chromosomes: segments carrying different genes move to a different chromosome, which can disrupt genes or cause problems in meiosis.

DUPLICATIONS AND DELETIONSGene dosage changesThey change the number of copies of genes, and so how much of their products the cell makes. Large duplications are usually harmful; small ones of one or a few genes can last for generations. Losing a region is usually worse than duplicating it, but a deletion can persist because the other homolog still carries the gene. A chromosome left with no centromere, or with two, is usually lost within a few divisions, because the spindle cannot move it properly.
GENE FAMILIESDuplication and divergenceRepeated duplication and divergence make families of related genes, such as the globin genes, or about 400 genes for odor receptors in humans, which let us tell so many smells apart.
INVERSIONSCommon when smallSmall inversions are common and may have almost no effect. Large ones can cause problems in meiosis. Inversions explain why the order of genes can differ even between closely related species.
TRANSLOCATIONSTrouble in meiosisThe cell still has every gene, so most have no effect on the organism. But in meiosis the two swapped chromosomes may not go to the same gamete, giving gametes with extra copies of some genes and missing others.
KEY TERMS · TAP ONE TO OPEN IT
Gene duplication

A mutation that gives an extra copy of a gene on a chromosome. The extra copy can collect mutations and often ends up with a new function.

Gene deletion

A mutation that leaves a chromosome missing an entire gene.

Inversion

A chromosome breaks (both DNA strands) and the piece reattaches in reverse orientation, changing the order of genes. If whole genes and their regulatory sequences are intact, it may have no effect.

Reciprocal translocation

Two non-homologous chromosomes break (both strands) and each broken piece attaches to the other chromosome. It may or may not have effects, depending on where the breaks are.

WRONG NUMBERS

Nondisjunction: extra or missing chromosomes

Nondisjunction is the failure of homologs or sister chromatids to separate. It can happen in mitosis, meiosis I or meiosis II. In meiosis it gives gametes with an extra or missing chromosome, and the zygote they make is aneuploid.3,2,4

INTERACTIVE · DRAWN WITH CHROMOSOME 22 AND THE X AND Y

Nondisjunction of X and Y in a male germ cell

Tap the buttons, or Next, to click through all 4
NORMAL MEIOSISEvery sperm has 23X and Y are a pair: they separate in meiosis I. Sister chromatids separate in meiosis II. Every sperm gets one chromosome 22 and either an X or a Y.
MEIOSIS I NONDISJUNCTIONHomologs fail to separateX and Y go to the same pole. All four sperm are abnormal: two with X, Y and 22 (24 chromosomes in humans) and two with no sex chromosome (22).
MEIOSIS II NONDISJUNCTIONSister chromatids fail to separateMeiosis I was normal, but in one cell the Y's sister chromatids stay together. Two sperm are normal, one has two Y's (24) and one has none (22).
FERTILIZATIONAn aneuploid zygoteA sperm with X and Y + a normal egg (X) = 47, XXY: one extra chromosome (Klinefelter syndrome). A sperm with no sex chromosome + an egg = 45, X: one missing (Turner syndrome).
Check yourself: What happens in meiosis I or II to give a gamete with extra or missing chromosomes, and what if it fuses with a normal gamete?

Meiosis I: a homologous pair fails to separate, so both members go to one cell; all four gametes are abnormal (two n + 1, two n − 1). Meiosis II: sister chromatids fail to separate; two gametes are normal, one n + 1, one n − 1. Fused with a normal gamete, an n + 1 gamete gives a trisomic zygote (2n + 1, such as trisomy 21) and an n − 1 gamete a monosomic one (2n − 1): both aneuploid. Most aneuploid embryos do not survive.

POLYPLOIDYIf an entire set of chromosomes fails to separate, a gamete can be diploid. Fertilized by a normal gamete, it gives a triploid (3n) zygote: polyploidy. Common in plants.
COMMON MIX-UPAneuploidy = one or a few whole chromosomes too many or too few (47, 45). Polyploidy = whole extra sets (3n, 4n).
KARYOTYPEWHAT IS DIFFERENTSYNDROME
47, +21An extra chromosome 21Down syndrome
47, +13An extra chromosome 13Patau syndrome
47, +18An extra chromosome 18Edwards syndrome
47, XXXAn extra XNone
47, XYYAn extra YNone
45, XA missing XTurner syndrome
47, XXYAn extra XKlinefelter syndrome
HOW COMMONAbout 1 in 155 birthshas a major chromosome anomaly; about half are aneuploidies from nondisjunction. Most aneuploid embryos are lost early in development, so these are only the survivors.
MOTHER'S AGERisk rises with ageDown syndrome affects about 1 in 750 births overall, but the risk is about 50 times higher for mothers aged 45 to 50 than for mothers aged 15 to 20.
SEX CHROMOSOMESMilder effectsExtra or missing sex chromosomes have fewer effects than extra autosomes: the Y carries few genes, and in females all X chromosomes but one are inactivated.
Check yourself: Fiona (FfGg; F and G on different chromosomes) makes eggs. Meiosis I is normal, but in meiosis II the chromosome carrying G fails to separate. Which egg is NOT possible: f, FGG, fgg, Fgg or FGg?

FGg. In meiosis II the two sister chromatids fail to separate, and sisters are identical (no crossing over), so an egg can get GG, gg or no G chromosome at all, never G with g. f (no G chromosome), FGG, fgg and Fgg are all possible.

KEY TERMS · TAP ONE TO OPEN IT
Nondisjunction

The failure of homologous chromosomes and/or sister chromatids to separate properly during cell division: in mitosis, meiosis I or meiosis II.

Aneuploidy

Too many or too few whole chromosomes in a cell. It results from nondisjunction.

Polyploidy

Having more than two of each type of chromosome: triploid (3n), tetraploid (4n) and so on. Fertilization after nondisjunction of an entire genome can give a polyploid.

READ IT

Reading a karyotype

A karyotype shows a cell's condensed chromosomes, sorted into pairs from the longest to the shortest, with the sex chromosomes last. It is how extra or missing chromosomes are found.3

INTERACTIVE · THREE KARYOTYPES

Count, pair, check the sex chromosomes

Tap the buttons, or Next, to click through all 3
A TYPICAL MALE46, XY22 numbered pairs plus X and Y: 46 chromosomes, diploid. (A typical female is 46, XX.)
TRISOMY 2147, +21Three copies of chromosome 21: Down syndrome. It comes from nondisjunction of chromosome 21 in a parent's meiosis.
AN EXTRA X47, XXYTwo X chromosomes and a Y: Klinefelter syndrome, the result drawn in the section above.
Check yourself: What can you learn from a karyotype?

The number of chromosomes (normal 46, or aneuploid such as 47 or 45), whether they come in pairs (diploid, haploid or polyploid), the sex chromosomes (XX or XY), and large structural changes such as big deletions, duplications or translocations. You cannot see point mutations or which alleles a person carries.

Check yourself: A cell shows one of each chromosome 1 to 22 (each replicated), plus an X and a Y. What went wrong, and what is the result?

Process: nondisjunction of the X and Y in meiosis I of a male germ cell: the pair went to the same pole. Result: a haploid cell with 24 chromosomes instead of 23; its sperm would give an XXY zygote with a normal egg.

HOW DO WE KNOW?

Mutations are random: the Lederbergs' experiment

Treat bacteria with an antibiotic and the survivors are resistant. Did the antibiotic cause resistance mutations, or were resistant cells already there? Esther and Joshua Lederberg tested it in 1952 with replica plating.5,6,4

INTERACTIVE · REPLICA PLATING

Were the resistant bacteria there first?

Tap the buttons, or Next, to click through all 4
SETUPCopy the coloniesBacteria grow on a master plate with no antibiotic; each colony is thousands of identical cells from a single cell. A sterile velvet disk picks up cells from every colony and stamps them, in the same positions, onto a fresh plate that contains antibiotic (the selective plate). A copy stamped onto a plate without antibiotic is the control: every colony grows there.
RESULT 1Only two colonies growOn the antibiotic plate, only the colonies at two spots (X and Y) grow. The rest die.
GO BACKFind the same spots on the originalBecause the stamp kept positions, the Lederbergs could find the colonies at X and Y on the original plate, which had never touched antibiotic.
RESULT 2They were already resistantFrom those original colonies the Lederbergs grew a pure culture of antibiotic-resistant bacteria, although those cells had never met the antibiotic. The resistance mutations existed before exposure. The antibiotic did not cause them: it selected them.
Check yourself: A population of bacteria is treated with an antibiotic, and every surviving cell is resistant. Why?

Some cells already had resistance mutations, and only they survived and reproduced. The antibiotic did not cause the mutations.

WHAT IT SHOWSMutations are random with respect to an organism's needs: they do not happen because they would be useful. The environment does not create mutations; it selects among them. (Mutagens raise the overall rate of mutation, but not of the useful ones in particular.)
WHO INHERITS IT

Germ-line vs. somatic mutations

A mutation can happen in any cell, but only those in germ cells can reach the next generation.6,4

INTERACTIVE · TWO KINDS

Passed on, or not

Tap a button to explore
SOMATIC MUTATIONStays in the bodyA mutation in a body cell is passed to that cell's descendants by mitosis (a patch of skin, a sectored flower, sometimes a cancer), but not to offspring, because gametes don't come from that cell.
GERM-LINE MUTATIONPassed to offspringA mutation in a germ cell can end up in a gamete. A child who grows from that gamete has the mutation in every cell, including its own germ cells, so it can be passed on again.
TAP ONEWhere did it happen?Tap a somatic mutation, then a germ-line mutation.
Check yourself: Why are germ-line, but not somatic, mutations passed to the next generation?

Offspring come only from gametes, and gametes are made only from germ cells by meiosis. A mutation in a somatic cell is not in any germ cell, so no gamete carries it.

SECTORED FLOWERSA somatic mutation you can seeA mutation in a flower-color gene in one cell is copied into all that cell's descendants, painting a patch, or sector, of a different color.
CANCERSomatic mutations adding upMost cancers come from somatic mutations. Usually two, three or more mutations in different genes (for one colon cancer: APC, Ras and p53) must build up in the same cell lineage. They are not passed on, except when a family carries a germ-line mutation in one of these genes, which starts every cell one step along.
GO DEEPER · FROM THE TEXTBOOKSometimes one step toward cancer is inherited: a germ-line mutation in a cancer gene is in every cell from birth, so fewer new somatic mutations are needed. Major inherited risk factors are mutations in APC, Ras and p53 (colon cancer) and BRCA1 and BRCA2 (breast and ovarian cancer). Environment adds risk too: tobacco smoke is the biggest risk factor for lung cancer, and UV light (sun, tanning beds) for skin cancer.
Check yourself: What is the difference between a somatic and a germ-line mutation?

Where it happens: a somatic mutation is in a body cell and is not passed to offspring; a germ-line mutation is in a germ cell and can be passed to offspring.

Check yourself: True or false: a mutation in a person's skin cells that causes skin cancer has a 50% chance of being passed to any child they have later.

False. Skin cells are somatic cells. Gametes come only from germ cells, so a skin-cell mutation cannot reach a child.

KEY TERMS · TAP ONE TO OPEN IT
Somatic mutation

A change in the DNA sequence of a somatic (body) cell. It is passed to that cell's descendants but not to offspring.

Germ-line mutation

A change in the DNA sequence of a germ cell. It can be passed down to offspring.

PUT IT TOGETHER

Important ideas about mutations

Genotype is an organism's genetic makeup; phenotype is its observable traits. Different alleles are different DNA sequences, and mutations make them. Whether a mutation changes the phenotype depends on how it affects gene function, and often on the environment.6,4

IDEA 1Spontaneous and rareMutations are rare events, increased by mutagens.
IDEA 2By chanceThey happen during DNA replication, mitosis, meiosis or binary fission.
IDEA 3RandomThey do not occur because of an organism's needs (the Lederbergs).
IDEA 4Make evolution possibleThey create genetic variation, the raw material of evolution.
MUTATIONS IN...USUAL EFFECT
Most noncoding DNANeutral
Most missense, nonsense and frameshift mutationsDeleterious
A few mutations, coding or noncodingBeneficial
Somatic cellsNot passed to offspring
Germ cellsPassed to offspring
Check yourself: How can a mutation in a noncoding region be beneficial?

Noncoding DNA includes regulatory sequences such as enhancers that control how much of a gene is made. In people from dairy-farming regions, mutations in an enhancer upstream of the lactase gene keep it switched on in adults (lactase persistence), so they can digest milk: a beneficial mutation with no change to the protein at all.

Check yourself: When and where do mutations occur, and which kind (neutral, deleterious, advantageous) is most common?

By chance, mostly during DNA replication (and during mitosis, meiosis and binary fission), in the DNA of any cell, which in eukaryotes is mostly the nuclear DNA in the nucleus. Neutral is the most common: no effect on fitness. Deleterious lowers fitness; advantageous (beneficial) raises it and is rare.

SORT THEM

Every mutation type, sorted

Four questions from class: which types can be point mutations, which must be in coding regions, which can be in noncoding regions, and which are chromosomal?2,4

TYPEPOINT OR CHROMOSOMALCODING ONLY?NOTES
SubstitutionPointNoCan be synonymous, missense or nonsense in a gene
IndelPointNoNot a multiple of 3 in a gene = frameshift
SynonymousPoint (a substitution)YesSame amino acid
Missense = nonsynonymousPoint (a substitution)YesDifferent amino acid
NonsensePoint (a substitution)YesEarly stop; not missense
FrameshiftPoint (an indel)YesShifts the reading frame; not missense or nonsense
Gene duplicationChromosomalNoExtra copy; can evolve a new function
Gene deletionChromosomalNoA whole gene missing
InversionChromosomalNoSegment reversed; may have no effect
Reciprocal translocationChromosomalNoNon-homologous chromosomes swap pieces
Nondisjunction → aneuploidyChromosomalNoWhole chromosomes too many or too few
Neutral · deleterious · advantageousEitherNoDescribe the effect on fitness, not the kind of change
COMMON MIX-UPNeutral, deleterious and advantageous (beneficial) are not types of change: they describe a mutation's effect on fitness. Any type of mutation can be any of the three, though some types are usually one of them.

Lock it in · Part 5

  1. Chromosomal mutations: gene duplication (extra copy, can gain a new function), gene deletion, inversion (order reversed), reciprocal translocation (non-homologous chromosomes swap pieces).
  2. Nondisjunction (homologs in meiosis I, or sisters in meiosis II, fail to separate) gives gametes with n + 1 or n − 1; the zygote is aneuploid (47, XXY; 47, +21; 45, X). A whole set → polyploidy.
  3. A karyotype shows number, pairs, sex chromosomes and large changes, not point mutations.
  4. The Lederbergs' replica plating: resistant colonies existed before the antibiotic. Mutations are random; the environment selects.
  5. Only germ-line mutations are passed to offspring; somatic ones stay in the body.
  6. Most mutations are neutral; a noncoding mutation can be beneficial by changing gene regulation (lactase persistence).
