Vocab · 58 terms
Advantageous mutation A change in coding or noncoding DNA that has a positive effect on an organism's fitness. Same as beneficial.
Aneuploidy Too many or too few whole chromosomes in a cell. It results from nondisjunction.
Asexual reproduction Reproduction by one parent alone. The offspring are genetically identical to the parent, except for new mutations.
Allele One version of a gene. Different alleles have different DNA sequences. A diploid cell has two alleles of each gene, one on each homolog; a gamete has one.
Beneficial mutation A change in coding or noncoding DNA that has a positive effect on an organism's fitness. Same as advantageous.
Bivalent The same thing as a tetrad: two replicated homologs paired side by side in meiosis I, held together by chiasmata.
Chiasmata Plural of chiasma: the X-shaped points where two non-sister chromatids of a bivalent have crossed over. They form in prophase I (1 to 3 per chromosome) and hold the homologs together.
Deleterious mutation A change in coding or noncoding DNA that has a negative effect on an organism's fitness.
Diploid Having two of each type of chromosome (2n), one set from each parent, so chromosomes come in homologous pairs.
Egg The female gamete: a large haploid cell. In humans it carries 22 autosomes and an X.
Fertilization The fusion of a haploid egg and a haploid sperm into a diploid zygote. It restores the chromosome number: n + n = 2n.
Frameshift mutation Coding regions only: an indel of a number of bases that is not a multiple of 3, which shifts the mRNA's reading frame from that point on. Not counted as missense, even if it makes an early stop.
Gametes Haploid reproductive cells made by meiosis: eggs and sperm. Each carries one allele of every gene.
Gene deletion A mutation that leaves a chromosome missing an entire gene.
Gene duplication A mutation that gives an extra copy of a gene on a chromosome. The extra copy can collect mutations and often ends up with a new function.
Germ cells The diploid cells that give rise to gametes by meiosis, in the ovaries and testes in humans. (The textbook also counts the gametes themselves as germ cells.)
Germ-line mutation A change in the DNA sequence of a germ cell. It can be passed down to offspring.
Haploid Having one of each type of chromosome: one complete set (n).
Homologous chromosome One of a pair of chromosomes similar in size, shape and gene content, one inherited from each parent. They carry the same genes at the same loci, but can carry different alleles.
Indel (insertion/deletion) Insertion or deletion of one or more base pairs, in coding or noncoding DNA. A type of point mutation.
Independent assortment Each homologous pair lines up at metaphase I independently of the others, so each gamete gets a random mix of maternal and paternal chromosomes: 2ⁿ combinations.
Inversion A chromosome breaks (both DNA strands) and the piece reattaches in reverse orientation, changing the order of genes. If whole genes and their regulatory sequences are intact, it may have no effect.
Locus The place on a chromosome where a particular gene sits. Homologous chromosomes carry the same genes at the same loci (plural of locus).
Meiosis The cell division that turns one diploid germ cell into four haploid gametes: one round of DNA replication, then two divisions, meiosis I and meiosis II. The gametes are genetically different from the parent cell and from each other.
Metaphase I and II Metaphase I: the bivalents line up across the middle of the cell, homologs facing opposite poles. Metaphase II: in each haploid cell the replicated chromosomes line up one by one, as in mitosis.
Missense mutation Coding regions only: a substitution that gives an mRNA codon for a different amino acid. Means the same as nonsynonymous.
Neutral mutation A change in coding or noncoding DNA that has no effect on an organism's fitness. The most common kind.
Nonsense mutation Coding regions only: a substitution (not an indel) that gives an early stop codon in the mRNA. Not counted as missense or nonsynonymous.
Nonsynonymous mutation Coding regions only: a substitution that gives an mRNA codon for a different amino acid. Means the same as missense.
Nuclear DNA The DNA in the nucleus of a eukaryotic cell, organized into linear chromosomes. Meiosis shares out the nuclear DNA.
Point mutation A small change of one or a few nucleotides at one place in the genome, in coding or noncoding DNA. Substitutions and indels are point mutations. (The textbook uses a narrower definition: a change in a single nucleotide.)
Polyploidy Having more than two of each type of chromosome: triploid (3n), tetraploid (4n) and so on. Fertilization after nondisjunction of an entire genome can give a polyploid.
Reciprocal translocation Two non-homologous chromosomes break (both strands) and each broken piece attaches to the other chromosome. It may or may not have effects, depending on where the breaks are.
Recombination New combinations of maternal and paternal alleles on one chromosome, made by crossing over between non-sister chromatids in prophase I.
Sexual reproduction Reproduction in which meiosis makes haploid gametes and two gametes, usually from two parents, fuse at fertilization. Each offspring gets one set of chromosomes from each parent.
Sister chromatids The two copies in a replicated chromosome, made in S phase. They are identical, except for a new mutation or a crossover.
Somatic mutation A change in the DNA sequence of a somatic (body) cell. It is passed to that cell's descendants but not to offspring.
Substitution Replacement of one nucleotide with another, in coding or noncoding DNA. A type of point mutation.
Synonymous mutation Coding regions only: a substitution that gives an mRNA codon for the same amino acid. The protein does not change.
Sperm The male gamete: a small haploid cell with a flagellum. In humans it carries 22 autosomes and either an X or a Y.
Tetrad A pair of replicated homologous chromosomes joined together in prophase I: four chromatids. Also called a bivalent.
Zygote The diploid cell formed at fertilization, the first cell of a new organism. It divides by mitosis to build the body.
Chromosome A structure made of DNA and proteins that carries the cell's hereditary information (genes).
Sex chromosome A chromosome associated with an individual's sex: X and Y in humans (females XX, males XY).
Autosome Any chromosome that is not a sex chromosome: chromosomes 1 to 22 in humans.
Unreplicated chromosome A chromosome that is a single copy: one DNA molecule (one thread).
Replicated chromosome A chromosome that has been copied: two sister chromatids joined at one centromere.
Non-sister chromatids Chromatids that belong to different homologous chromosomes. Crossing over happens between non-sister chromatids.
Haploid number n: the number of different types of chromosomes in a cell. Humans: n = 23.
Diploid number 2n: the number of chromosomes in a diploid cell. Humans: 2n = 46.
Ploidy The number of each type of chromosome present: the number of complete sets.
Nondisjunction The failure of homologous chromosomes and/or sister chromatids to separate properly during cell division: in mitosis, meiosis I or meiosis II.
Genotype The genetic makeup of a cell or organism: which alleles it carries.
Phenotype An organism's observable characteristics or traits (appearance, physiology, behavior). It results from the genotype interacting with the environment.
Polymorphism A genetic difference among individuals that is present in many individuals of a population. Alleles correspond to different DNA sequences, polymorphisms, in a gene.
Homozygous Having two copies of the same allele of a gene (for example AA).
Heterozygous Having two different alleles of a gene (for example AS).
Polar body A small cell made by the unequal division of the cytoplasm in female meiosis. It gets very little cytoplasm and does not become an egg.

Notes

Everything you are expected to know for this module, in the order the learning objectives ask for it. Read it once, then use the checklist at the end.

IN THESE NOTES1 · Sexual vs. asexual reproduction2 · Mitosis, meiosis and the life cycle3 · Meiosis, stage by stage4 · Counting, karyotypes and large numbers5 · Crossing over and genetic variation6 · Mutations and genetic variation7 · Types of mutations8 · How mutations affect the phenotype9 · Exam checklist
THE BIG IDEA

Meiosis turns one diploid germ cell into four haploid gametes: one DNA replication, then two divisions. Meiosis I separates homologs; meiosis II separates sister chromatids. Crossing over, independent assortment and random fertilization make every gamete and zygote different, but only mutation makes new alleles.

SECTION 1OBJECTIVE 3

Sexual vs. asexual reproduction

  • Asexual: one parent; offspring identical to the parent, except new mutations. Examples: bacteria and archaea (binary fission), yeast (budding), strawberry runners, hydra (budding), aphids, whiptail lizards.
  • Sexual: meiosis makes haploid gametes; two gametes fuse at fertilization; each offspring is a new mixture of both parents.
  • Most organisms reproduce sexually at least part of the time. Even bacteria and archaea exchange DNA, for example by conjugation.
SEXUALASEXUAL
AdvantagesHigh genetic variability; rapid adaptation to new environments and parasites; recombination helps eliminate deleterious mutationsSaves energy; no courtship or mates; faster population growth
DisadvantagesEnergy costly; courtship takes time and resources; only females produce offspringLow genetic variability; adapting is difficult; deleterious mutations removed only by death
KEY CONSEQUENCEIncreased genetic variation is the key consequence of sexual reproduction, and variation is what lets a species adapt.
SECTION 2OBJECTIVES 1, 2, 4 AND 5

Mitosis, meiosis and the life cycle

  • Mitosis (somatic cells): 2 identical diploid cells, for growth, development, repair and asexual reproduction.
  • Meiosis (only germ cells, in ovaries and testes): 4 haploid gametes, genetically different, for sexual reproduction.
  • Life cycle: diploid zygote → mitosis builds the body → germ cells undergo meiosis → haploid egg and sperm → fertilization (n + n = 2n) → a new zygote.
  • Germ cells exist to make gametes; only their DNA reaches the next generation.
  • Genetic information: somatic and germ cells are diploid with the same DNA (both alleles of every gene); each gamete is haploid with one allele of each gene, a different mix in every gamete.
  • Females: 1 egg + 3 polar bodies (unequal cytoplasm). Males: 4 sperm.
MITOSISMEIOSIS
WhereSomatic cellsOnly germ cells
DNA replications11
Divisions12
Daughter cells24
Chromosome numberSame (2n → 2n)Half (2n → n)
Daughters vs. parentIdenticalDifferent
Homologs pair, cross over, separateNoYes, meiosis I
Sister chromatids separateYesYes, meiosis II
SECTION 3OBJECTIVES 6 AND 7

Meiosis, stage by stage

  • Same phases as mitosis, twice: prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase, first as meiosis I, then again as meiosis II. Meiosis I is the new part (homologs pair, cross over and separate); meiosis II works like mitosis.
  • S phase (before meiosis): every chromosome replicated into 2 sister chromatids. The only replication.
  • Prophase I: chromosomes start as long, thin, tangled threads (each already 2 sister chromatids); homologs find each other and zip together along their length while still long (synapsis) into a bivalent or tetrad (2 chromosomes, 4 chromatids); crossing over between non-sister chromatids, seen as chiasmata; only then do they condense into the tidy shapes. The only time homologs pair.
  • Metaphase I: bivalents line up across the middle, homologs facing opposite poles. Anaphase I: homologs separate; sisters stay together. Telophase I + cytokinesis: 2 haploid cells.
  • Meiosis II (like mitosis): metaphase II, chromosomes line up one by one; anaphase II, sister chromatids separate; telophase II, 4 haploid cells.
  • Ploidy: diploid before and during meiosis I; haploid after meiosis I and after meiosis II.
  • Draw: before S, after S, metaphase I, metaphase II, after meiosis I, after meiosis II, in two colors. Sister chromatids are present at metaphase I and II; homologs only at metaphase I.
MEIOSIS IReductional: separates homologs, 2n → n.
MEIOSIS IIEquational: separates sister chromatids, n → n.
SECTION 4OBJECTIVES 8 AND 9

Counting, karyotypes and large numbers

STAGEPLOIDY2n = 2HUMAN
G1 germ cell2n2 chromosomes · 2 DNA46 · 46
After S2n2 · 446 · 92
Metaphase I2n2 · 4 (1 bivalent)46 · 92 (23 bivalents)
After meiosis I (each)n1 · 223 · 46
After meiosis II (each)n1 · 123 · 23
  • Chromosomes = centromeres; DNA molecules = chromatids. Horse 2n = 64 → gametes with 32.
  • A karyotype shows the number of chromosomes, pairs (ploidy), sex chromosomes (XX or XY) and large structural changes; not point mutations or alleles.
  • Humans: 46 = 22 pairs of autosomes + XX or XY. 47, +21 = Down syndrome; 47, XXY = Klinefelter; 45, X = Turner.
SECTION 5OBJECTIVES 10 AND 11

Crossing over and genetic variation

  • Crossing over happens in prophase I between non-sister chromatids of homologs at chiasmata (1 to 3 per chromosome). Matching segments swap precisely; the result is recombinant chromatids with new combinations of maternal and paternal alleles (A D + a d → A d and a D).
  • Independent assortment (metaphase I): each homologous pair orients at random, so 2ⁿ combinations; 2n = 4 gives 4; humans 2²³ ≈ 8 million.
  • Random fertilization: 2ⁿ × 2ⁿ zygotes; a human couple ≈ 70 trillion, before crossing over.
  • Sister chromatids can carry different alleles after a mutation in S phase or a crossover; non-sister chromatids can differ because they came from different parents.
A CATCHThese three only shuffle existing alleles. New alleles come only from mutation.
SECTION 6OBJECTIVES 12, 13 AND 14

Mutations and genetic variation

  • A mutation is any heritable change in DNA: the ultimate source of genetic variation, and so of evolution.
  • They happen by chance, mostly as copying errors in DNA replication (also in mitosis, meiosis, binary fission); mutagens raise the rate. A mismatch that escapes repair becomes permanent at the next replication.
  • Rare per nucleotide (about 1 in 10 billion per replication), common per genome (about 60 new per human zygote, most from the father).
  • Germ-line mutations can be passed to offspring; somatic mutations stay in the body (sectored flowers, most cancers).
  • Random: the Lederbergs' replica plating found antibiotic-resistant colonies that had never met the antibiotic. The environment selects mutations; it does not cause them.
SECTION 7OBJECTIVE 15

Types of mutations

TYPECATEGORYCODING ONLY?WHAT IT IS
SubstitutionPointNoOne nucleotide replaced
IndelPointNoOne or more base pairs inserted or deleted
SynonymousPointYesCodon for the same amino acid
Missense = nonsynonymousPointYesCodon for a different amino acid
NonsensePointYesEarly stop codon (a substitution)
FrameshiftPointYesIndel not a multiple of 3
Gene duplicationChromosomalNoExtra copy; can evolve a new function
Gene deletionChromosomalNoA whole gene missing
InversionChromosomalNoSegment reversed; may have no effect
Reciprocal translocationChromosomalNoNon-homologous chromosomes swap pieces
Nondisjunction → aneuploidyChromosomalNoToo many or too few whole chromosomes
PolyploidyChromosomalNoWhole extra sets (3n, 4n)
  • Point mutation (this course): one or a few nucleotides, so substitutions and indels. The textbook's narrower meaning is a single-nucleotide change.
  • Nonsense is not missense or nonsynonymous. A frameshift is not missense, even if it creates a stop. An indel of 3 is not missense.
  • Nondisjunction: meiosis I (homologs) → all 4 gametes abnormal; meiosis II (sisters) → 2 normal, 1 n + 1, 1 n − 1. With a normal gamete: a trisomic or monosomic zygote.
SECTION 8OBJECTIVE 16

How mutations affect the phenotype

  • Synonymous mutations don't change the amino acid, so the protein and the phenotype are unchanged.
  • Missense changes one amino acid, which can change folding and function (the sickle-cell S allele: Glu → Val). Nonsense cuts the protein short; frameshifts scramble it. Both are nearly always deleterious.
  • Most noncoding mutations are neutral, but mutations in regulatory sequences can matter, even be beneficial (lactase persistence).
  • Genotype + environment → phenotype. Alleles are different DNA sequences (polymorphisms). Effects can depend on homozygous vs. heterozygous (SS vs. AS) and on the environment (malaria).
NEUTRALMost noncoding mutations; synonymous ones.
DELETERIOUSMost missense, nonsense and frameshift mutations.
BENEFICIALA few, coding or noncoding.
SECTION 9

Exam checklist

You're ready when you can:

  • Compare sexual and asexual reproduction, with examples and the advantages and disadvantages of each.
  • Place mitosis, meiosis and fertilization in a life cycle, and say what genetic information somatic cells, germ cells and gametes carry.
  • Name the phases of meiosis I and II, and say which work like mitosis and which are new.
  • Draw meiosis for 2n = 2 (and 2n = 4): before and after S, metaphase I and II, and the cells after meiosis I and II, labelling sister chromatids and homologs.
  • Give the ploidy and the chromosome and DNA counts at every stage, for any 2n.
  • Read a karyotype: count, pairs, sex chromosomes, aneuploidy.
  • Explain when crossing over happens and what it does to alleles; calculate 2ⁿ and 2ⁿ × 2ⁿ.
  • Explain why only germ-line mutations are inherited, and describe the Lederbergs' experiment.
  • Identify any mutation from a sequence or drawing: synonymous, missense, nonsense, indel, frameshift, duplication, deletion, inversion, translocation, nondisjunction.
  • Explain why synonymous mutations don't change the phenotype and how the other types can.
COMMON MIX-UPMeiosis I separates homologs (2n → n); meiosis II separates sister chromatids. Crossing over is between non-sister chromatids of homologs; a translocation is between non-homologous chromosomes. And nonsense is never missense; a frameshift is never missense or nonsense.

Infographics

Every diagram from the flow charts in one place, without the reading in between. Start with the one-page map, then scan the rest.

INFOGRAPHIC 1 · THE WHOLE MODULE ON ONE PAGE
MODULE 3.2 · PART 1

Reproduction and the job of meiosis

Why do most organisms bother with sex, and which cells make the gametes?

1Two ways to reproduce
Reproduction is a basic property of every living thing. There are two ways to do it, and they differ in how many parents are involved and in how alike the offspring are.
2Why bother with sex?
Sexual reproduction costs more, yet most organisms do it at least some of the time. The payoff is genetic variation.
3Where meiosis fits
Meiosis happens in only one kind of cell and at one point in the life cycle: germ cells, when they make gametes. Mitosis does everything else.1,2
4Homologs, chromatids and ploidy
Before following chromosomes through meiosis, get the words straight. Meiosis only works in a cell that has homologous pairs: two of each kind of chromosome, one from each parent.3
MODULE 3.2 · PART 2

Meiosis, step by step

How does one diploid germ cell end up as four haploid gametes, with only one round of DNA replication?

1Phases of meiosis: the same four as mitosis, run twice
If meiosis looks a lot like mitosis, that is because it uses the same phases: prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase. Mitosis goes through them once. Meiosis goes through them twice, meiosis I and then meiosis II, after a single round of DNA replication.1,2
2Meiosis, stage by stage
One diploid germ cell, one pair of chromosomes (2n = 2), all the way to four gametes. Watch the counts at the bottom: one round of DNA replication, then two divisions.1,2
2Synapsis, bivalents and chiasmata: prophase I as it really looks
Most diagrams start prophase I with neat X-shaped pairs. Real prophase I starts as a tangle: the chromosomes "first appear as long, thin threads present throughout the nucleus," and the homologs find each other and pair up while they're still long. The tidy shapes only appear at the end.1,2
3The drawings to know
Exams ask you to draw meiosis: before and after DNA replication, at metaphase I and II, and the daughter cells after meiosis I and meiosis II, and to point out sister chromatids and homologs. Here are all six.
4Ploidy and counts, before, during and after
The same counting rules as mitosis: chromosomes = centromeres, DNA molecules = chromatids. What changes in meiosis is the ploidy.
5Meiosis vs. mitosis
Meiosis II looks like mitosis. The big differences are all in meiosis I: homologs pair, cross over and separate.1
6Same meiosis, different cytoplasm
Meiosis shares out the chromosomes the same way in both sexes, but in animals the cytoplasm divides very differently.1
MODULE 3.2 · PART 3

Where genetic variation comes from

Two siblings get their chromosomes from the same two parents. Why aren't they identical?

1Three ways meiosis and fertilization make variation
Genetic variation, the genetic differences among individuals in a population, is critical to a species' long-term survival: a species can only adapt to new or changing environments if it has variation. Darwin saw it in 1859: individual differences are what natural selection works on.1,2
2Crossing over and recombination
Crossing over happens in prophase I, while the homologs are paired as a bivalent. Usually 1 to 3 chiasmata form per chromosome.3,2
3Independent assortment
At metaphase I, each pair lines up on its own, maternal homolog facing one pole or the other at random. With n pairs there are 2ⁿ combinations. One human can make gametes with 2²³, about 8 million, different combinations of chromosomes.3,2
4Random fertilization
Any of a mother's eggs can meet any of a father's sperm. For humans, one couple can make 2²³ × 2²³, about 70 trillion, unique zygotes, and that is without the extra variety from crossing over.2
MODULE 3.2 · PART 4

Point mutations

Every allele began as a mutation. What kinds of small changes can happen to DNA, and what do they do to a protein?

1What is a mutation?
A mutation is any heritable change in the genetic material: it is stable and is passed on through cell division (meiosis, mitosis or binary fission). Mutation is the ultimate source of genetic variation: every allele began as one.1,2
2How a copying error becomes a mutation, and how often
Most mistakes in DNA replication are fixed right away: DNA polymerase proofreads, and repair enzymes catch most of the rest. A fixed mistake is not a mutation. A mutation is a mistake that escapes repair and is then copied.1
3One letter swapped: synonymous, missense, nonsense
A substitution replaces one nucleotide with another. In a coding region, what it does depends on how the mRNA codon changes. 64 codons code for 20 amino acids and 3 stops, so most amino acids have several codons (you don't need to memorize the code).3,1,2
4Letters added or lost: indels and frameshifts
An indel is an insertion or deletion of one or more base pairs. The name covers both because, comparing two sequences, a gap in one could be an insertion in the other or a deletion in the first. Unlike a substitution, an indel changes the length of the DNA.3,1,2
5Which types need a coding region?
Most of the human genome does not code for protein: about 2.5% does, and more than 90% of the nucleotides seem free to vary without harm. That is why each of us can carry about 60 new mutations and be fine. A mutation in noncoding DNA usually has no effect, but some noncoding DNA regulates genes, and a mutation there can matter.1,3
6From a change in DNA to a change in the organism
Genetic variation matters for evolution because it creates heritable differences in phenotype. But many mutations change no trait at all, and the ones that do can have different effects depending on the rest of the genotype and on the environment.1,2
MODULE 3.2 · PART 5

Chromosomal mutations, and where mutations come from

What happens when whole chunks of chromosomes, or whole chromosomes, go wrong, and do mutations happen because an organism needs them?

1Chromosomal mutations
Some mutations affect large regions: hundreds of thousands to millions of nucleotides, often big enough to see under a microscope. They change how many copies of genes there are, or where the genes sit.1,2
2Nondisjunction: extra or missing chromosomes
Nondisjunction is the failure of homologs or sister chromatids to separate. It can happen in mitosis, meiosis I or meiosis II. In meiosis it gives gametes with an extra or missing chromosome, and the zygote they make is aneuploid.3,2,4
3Reading a karyotype
A karyotype shows a cell's condensed chromosomes, sorted into pairs from the longest to the shortest, with the sex chromosomes last. It is how extra or missing chromosomes are found.3
4Mutations are random: the Lederbergs' experiment
Treat bacteria with an antibiotic and the survivors are resistant. Did the antibiotic cause resistance mutations, or were resistant cells already there? Esther and Joshua Lederberg tested it in 1952 with replica plating.5,6,4
5Germ-line vs. somatic mutations
A mutation can happen in any cell, but only those in germ cells can reach the next generation.6,4
6Important ideas about mutations
Genotype is an organism's genetic makeup; phenotype is its observable traits. Different alleles are different DNA sequences, and mutations make them. Whether a mutation changes the phenotype depends on how it affects gene function, and often on the environment.6,4
7Every mutation type, sorted
Four questions from class: which types can be point mutations, which must be in coding regions, which can be in noncoding regions, and which are chromosomal?2,4

Asexual vs. sexual reproduction

Part 2 · Meiosis, step by step

Phases of meiosis: the same four as mitosis, run twice
INFOGRAPHIC 6
INTERACTIVE · ONE GRID, THREE COLUMNS

Mitosis vs. meiosis I vs. meiosis II, phase by phase

Tap a button to explore
SAME NAMESProphase, metaphase, anaphase, telophaseBoth divisions use the same four phases, with the same basic jobs: condense and build a spindle, line up in the middle, pull apart, then split into two cells.Mitosis runs through them once. Meiosis runs through them twice, so each phase name gets a I or a II. Both start after one interphase, where the DNA is copied once.
MEIOSIS I VS. MITOSISSame phases, different partnersThis is where meiosis is new. In prophase I the homologs pair up and cross over, which never happens in mitosis. In metaphase I they line up in pairs, not single file. MEIOSIS II VS. MITOSISMitosis again, with half the chromosomesMeiosis II follows straight on, with no S phase first. Each phase works just like mitosis: line up single file, then the sister chromatids separate.The difference is the starting cell: it is haploid, so the result is 4 haploid cells in all, and crossing over made every one different.

Meiosis, stage by stage
INFOGRAPHIC 7
INTERACTIVE · 9 STAGES · 2n = 2

From one germ cell to four gametes

Tap the buttons, or Next, to click through all 9
BEFORE MEIOSIS · G1A diploid germ cellOne homologous pair: pink from the mother with allele A, blue from the father with allele a. Each chromosome is one DNA molecule.
BEFORE MEIOSIS · S PHASEDNA replication, onceEvery chromosome is copied into two sister chromatids. This is the only round of DNA replication: there is none between meiosis I and II.
MEIOSIS I · PROPHASE IHomologs pair up and cross overChromosomes condense. The two homologs find each other and lie side by side (synapsis), forming a bivalent (tetrad). This is the only time homologous chromosomes pair.Non-sister chromatids exchange segments at a chiasma (crossing over): here the inner chromatids swap their tips. The nuclear envelope breaks down and the spindle forms.
MEIOSIS I · METAPHASE IPairs line up togetherEach bivalent lines up across the middle, its two homologs facing opposite poles. Spindle fibers from one pole attach to one whole homolog.
MEIOSIS I · ANAPHASE IHomologs separateThe homologs are pulled to opposite poles. The centromeres do not split: sister chromatids stay together. This is what halves the chromosome number.
MEIOSIS I · TELOPHASE ITwo haploid cellsCytokinesis gives two cells, each with one replicated chromosome: haploid (n = 1), even though each chromosome still has 2 DNA molecules. One cell got the A homolog, the other the a homolog.
MEIOSIS II · METAPHASE IILine up one by oneIn each cell the replicated chromosome lines up on its own, as in mitosis. Fibers from both poles attach to its two sister chromatids.
MEIOSIS II · ANAPHASE IISister chromatids separateThe centromeres split and the sister chromatids are pulled apart. Each chromatid is now a chromosome.
MEIOSIS II · TELOPHASE IIFour haploid gametesFour haploid cells, each with one chromosome and one DNA molecule. Two carry A and two carry a, and because of crossing over no two are identical.
Synapsis, bivalents and chiasmata: prophase I as it really looks
INFOGRAPHIC 8
INTERACTIVE · 5 STAGES · 2n = 4

From tangled threads to bivalents

Tap the buttons, or Next, to click through all 5
EARLY PROPHASE ILong, thin, tangled threadsThe chromosomes start to condense and become visible as long, thin threads all through the nucleus, tangled together. DNA was already copied in S phase, so each thread is two sister chromatids (the two thin lines of one color).The threads are chromatin: DNA wound on proteins, not loose DNA.
SYNAPSISEach chromosome finds its homologEach chromosome pairs with its homolog, the same chromosome from the other parent, and the two zip together along their whole length, still long and wavy. This pairing is synapsis, and it happens only in meiosis.The zipped pair is a bivalent (tetrad): 2 chromosomes, 4 chromatids. Even X and Y pair, but only at their tips.
CROSSING OVERSwapping pieces while zippedWhile the homologs are zipped, two non-sister chromatids (one pink, one blue) break at the same place and rejoin to each other's piece: crossing over. Matching segments are exchanged; usually no DNA is gained or lost.Only 2 of the 4 chromatids swap at each crossover. The spots stay visible as chiasmata (✕). Where they fall is essentially random; most bivalents get at least one (humans: about 50 to 60 per meiosis).
LATE PROPHASE INow it looks like the drawingsThe threads coil up short and thick, and the bivalents finally look like the familiar tidy pictures. The chiasmata hold each pair together until anaphase I.Still count centromeres. 2 bivalents = 4 centromeres = 4 chromosomes, and 8 chromatids. Crossing over moved DNA between chromatids but didn't change any count.
METAPHASE ITop or bottom is randomThe bivalents line up across the middle, one homolog facing each pole. Which one faces up is random, and each pair lines up independently of every other pair.That's independent assortment, the reason behind Mendel's law of independent assortment (Module 3.3).

Part 3 · Where genetic variation comes from

Crossing over and recombination
INFOGRAPHIC 12
INTERACTIVE · TWO GENES ON ONE CHROMOSOME

How a chiasma makes new combinations

Tap the buttons, or Next, to click through all 4
PROPHASE IThe homologs pair upThe mother's chromosome carries A and D; the father's carries a and d. Each is two sister chromatids.
A CHIASMA FORMSNon-sister chromatids crossTwo non-sister chromatids, one pink and one blue, break at the same place. The chiasma also holds the homologs together until anaphase I.
THEY SWAPMatching segments are exchangedThe broken ends rejoin the other chromatid. The exchange is precise: the same genes, in the same order, no DNA gained or lost. Only the alleles below the break are swapped.
THE RESULTRecombinant chromatidsTwo chromatids keep the parental combinations (A D and a d). Two are recombinant (A d and a D): combinations that neither parent's chromosome had. Each goes to a different gamete.
Independent assortment
INFOGRAPHIC 13
INTERACTIVE · 2n = 4

Two pairs, two ways to line up

Tap a button to explore
WAY 1Both maternal homologs face one polePink A and pink B go one way, blue a and blue b the other. Gametes: AB and ab.
WAY 2The short pair is flippedPink A goes with blue b, blue a with pink B. Gametes: Ab and aB.
ALL FOUR2² = 4 kinds of gameteTwo pairs, each with 2 orientations: 2 × 2 = 4 combinations. Each orientation is equally likely in every germ cell.
TAP ONEWhat assorts independently?The homologous pairs: how one pair lines up has no effect on how the other lines up.

Part 4 · Point mutations

What is a mutation?
INFOGRAPHIC 15
INTERACTIVE · WHERE IT LANDS DECIDES ITS EFFECT

Neutral, deleterious or beneficial

Tap a button to explore
NEUTRALNo effect on fitnessMost mutations in noncoding DNA are neutral, and so are synonymous mutations. Neutral is the most common kind.
DELETERIOUSLowers fitnessMost missense, nonsense and frameshift mutations are deleterious: they change or break a protein.
BENEFICIALRaises fitnessFew mutations, coding or noncoding, are beneficial (advantageous). Example: mutations in an enhancer that keep the lactase gene on in adults, so they can digest milk.
TAP ONEThree possible effectsWhether a mutation helps or harms depends on where it lands, and on the environment.
How a copying error becomes a mutation, and how often
INFOGRAPHIC 16
INTERACTIVE · 4 STEPS

From a mismatch to a mutation

Tap the buttons, or Next, to click through all 4
THE ORIGINALA T-A base pairA matches T and G matches C. Watch the highlighted T-A pair.
THE MISTAKEA G across from the TDuring replication, DNA polymerase puts a G across from the T. If proofreading and repair miss it, the new DNA has a T-G mismatch.
THE NEXT REPLICATIONEach strand becomes a templateThe T strand is copied into a normal T-A pair. The G strand is copied into a C-G pair.
PERMANENTA substitutionThe C-G pair is perfectly matched, so nothing looks wrong and it is copied faithfully from then on: T-A has been replaced by C-G, a substitution, a point mutation. A variant like this that becomes common in a population is a single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP).
One letter swapped: synonymous, missense, nonsense
INFOGRAPHIC 17
INTERACTIVE · ONE CODON, THREE SUBSTITUTIONS

Identify the mutation type

Tap the buttons, or Next, to click through all 4
THE ORIGINALTTA → UUA → leucineThe coding strand reads TTA, the template strand AAT, so the mRNA codon is UUA, which codes for leucine.
MISSENSE (NONSYNONYMOUS)UUA → GUA: valineA different amino acid. Missense and nonsynonymous mean the same thing. The protein may work worse, or not at all, depending on the change. (The sickle-cell allele is a missense mutation: glutamic acid to valine.)
NONSENSEUUA → UAA: STOPAn early stop codon: translation ends early and the protein is cut short, so it is nearly always nonfunctional. A nonsense mutation is not counted as missense or nonsynonymous.
SYNONYMOUSUUA → CUA: still leucineThe same amino acid, so the protein does not change and the phenotype does not change. Synonymous codons usually differ at the third position, though here it is the first. The textbook's example is in beta-globin: GAG → GAA, both glutamic acid.
Letters added or lost: indels and frameshifts
INFOGRAPHIC 18
INTERACTIVE · READ IT IN THREES

What a frameshift does

Tap the buttons, or Next, to click through all 4
THE READING FRAMEThree letters at a timeA ribosome reads mRNA in codons of three, starting from the start codon, just as you read this sentence in three-letter words.
INSERT 1 · FRAMESHIFTEverything after it changesOne extra letter shifts the frame: every word after it is gibberish. In DNA, every codon downstream codes for a different amino acid, often hitting an early stop.
DELETE 1 · FRAMESHIFTSame problemLosing one letter (or 2, 4, 5...) shifts the frame the other way. Any indel that is not a multiple of 3 is a frameshift.
INSERT 3 · IN FRAMEOne extra wordThree letters add exactly one codon: one extra amino acid (or one fewer for a deletion), and the rest of the protein is unchanged.
From a change in DNA to a change in the organism
INFOGRAPHIC 19
EXAMPLE · ONE GENE, THREE ALLELES

Hemoglobin's beta-globin gene

Tap a button to explore
ALLELE AThe most commonGAG codes for glutamic acid. People with two copies (homozygous AA) have typical hemoglobin.
ALLELE SOne base changed: a missense mutationGTG codes for valine. One amino acid changes the way the protein folds and works: SS causes sickle-cell anemia. AS (heterozygous) gives only a mild anemia, and where malaria is common it protects against malaria, so there it is beneficial. Where there is no malaria, it is harmful.
ALLELE CAnother missense mutationAAG codes for lysine. AC gives partial protection against malaria; CC gives more protection and only a very mild anemia.
TAP AN ALLELEHow a DNA change reaches the phenotypeDNA sequence → mRNA codon → amino acid sequence → how the protein folds → how it works → the trait. You don't need to memorize these alleles: they show the principle.

Part 5 · Chromosomal mutations, and where mutations come from

Chromosomal mutations
INFOGRAPHIC 20
INTERACTIVE · FOUR KINDS

Duplication, deletion, inversion, translocation

Tap the buttons, or Next, to click through all 4
GENE DUPLICATIONAn extra copyA segment appears twice. A duplicated gene's extra copy is free to collect mutations, and it often ends up coding for a protein with a new function. That is how gene families arise.
GENE DELETIONA missing pieceA chromosome loses a segment and the genes in it. Usually more harmful than a duplication of the same region.
INVERSIONFlipped aroundBoth DNA strands break in two places and the piece reattaches in reverse orientation, changing the order of genes. If whole genes and their regulatory sequences survive the breaks, it may have no effect.
RECIPROCAL TRANSLOCATIONTwo chromosomes swapTwo non-homologous chromosomes break (both strands), and each broken piece attaches to the other chromosome. It may or may not have effects, depending on where the breaks are and whether regulatory regions are hit.
Nondisjunction: extra or missing chromosomes
INFOGRAPHIC 21
INTERACTIVE · DRAWN WITH CHROMOSOME 22 AND THE X AND Y

Nondisjunction of X and Y in a male germ cell

Tap the buttons, or Next, to click through all 4
NORMAL MEIOSISEvery sperm has 23X and Y are a pair: they separate in meiosis I. Sister chromatids separate in meiosis II. Every sperm gets one chromosome 22 and either an X or a Y.
MEIOSIS I NONDISJUNCTIONHomologs fail to separateX and Y go to the same pole. All four sperm are abnormal: two with X, Y and 22 (24 chromosomes in humans) and two with no sex chromosome (22).
MEIOSIS II NONDISJUNCTIONSister chromatids fail to separateMeiosis I was normal, but in one cell the Y's sister chromatids stay together. Two sperm are normal, one has two Y's (24) and one has none (22).
FERTILIZATIONAn aneuploid zygoteA sperm with X and Y + a normal egg (X) = 47, XXY: one extra chromosome (Klinefelter syndrome). A sperm with no sex chromosome + an egg = 45, X: one missing (Turner syndrome).
Reading a karyotype
INFOGRAPHIC 22
INTERACTIVE · THREE KARYOTYPES

Count, pair, check the sex chromosomes

Tap the buttons, or Next, to click through all 3
A TYPICAL MALE46, XY22 numbered pairs plus X and Y: 46 chromosomes, diploid. (A typical female is 46, XX.)
TRISOMY 2147, +21Three copies of chromosome 21: Down syndrome. It comes from nondisjunction of chromosome 21 in a parent's meiosis.
AN EXTRA X47, XXYTwo X chromosomes and a Y: Klinefelter syndrome, the result drawn in the section above.
Mutations are random: the Lederbergs' experiment
INFOGRAPHIC 23
INTERACTIVE · REPLICA PLATING

Were the resistant bacteria there first?

Tap the buttons, or Next, to click through all 4
SETUPCopy the coloniesBacteria grow on a master plate with no antibiotic; each colony is thousands of identical cells from a single cell. A sterile velvet disk picks up cells from every colony and stamps them, in the same positions, onto a fresh plate that contains antibiotic (the selective plate). A copy stamped onto a plate without antibiotic is the control: every colony grows there.
RESULT 1Only two colonies growOn the antibiotic plate, only the colonies at two spots (X and Y) grow. The rest die.
GO BACKFind the same spots on the originalBecause the stamp kept positions, the Lederbergs could find the colonies at X and Y on the original plate, which had never touched antibiotic.
RESULT 2They were already resistantFrom those original colonies the Lederbergs grew a pure culture of antibiotic-resistant bacteria, although those cells had never met the antibiotic. The resistance mutations existed before exposure. The antibiotic did not cause them: it selected them.
Germ-line vs. somatic mutations
INFOGRAPHIC 24
INTERACTIVE · TWO KINDS

Passed on, or not

Tap a button to explore
SOMATIC MUTATIONStays in the bodyA mutation in a body cell is passed to that cell's descendants by mitosis (a patch of skin, a sectored flower, sometimes a cancer), but not to offspring, because gametes don't come from that cell.
GERM-LINE MUTATIONPassed to offspringA mutation in a germ cell can end up in a gamete. A child who grows from that gamete has the mutation in every cell, including its own germ cells, so it can be passed on again.
TAP ONEWhere did it happen?Tap a somatic mutation, then a germ-line mutation.

Meiosis & Mutations

How a germ cell halves its chromosomes to make gametes, why every gamete is different, and how mutations change DNA.

02 / 41 · MODULE 3.2 · PART 1 · THE QUESTION

Reproduction and the job of meiosis

Why do most organisms bother with sex, and which cells make the gametes?

03 / 41 · MODULE 3.2 · PART 1 · START HERE

Two ways to reproduce

Reproduction is a basic property of every living thing. There are two ways to do it, and they differ in how many parents are involved and in how alike the offspring are.

Tap a button to explore
ASEXUAL REPRODUCTIONOne parent, identical offspringOne parent makes offspring by mitosis (or, in prokaryotes, binary fission). Every offspring has the same DNA as the parent, except for new mutations.
SEXUAL REPRODUCTIONTwo parents, mixed offspringEach parent makes haploid gametes by meiosis, and two gametes fuse at fertilization. Each offspring gets half its chromosomes from each parent, so it is a new mixture, unlike either parent.
WHY IT MATTERSSexual populations grow more slowlyIn an asexual population every offspring can reproduce, so numbers can double every generation. In a sexual population only females produce new offspring, so it takes a pair to make each new individual.
TAP ONEHow many parents?Tap asexual, then sexual, then compare how fast each population grows.
04 / 41 · MODULE 3.2 · PART 1 · TRADE-OFFS

Why bother with sex?

Sexual reproduction costs more, yet most organisms do it at least some of the time. The payoff is genetic variation.

05 / 41 · MODULE 3.2 · PART 1 · THE LIFE CYCLE

Where meiosis fits

Meiosis happens in only one kind of cell and at one point in the life cycle: germ cells, when they make gametes. Mitosis does everything else.1,2

Tap a button to explore
MEIOSISGerm cells make gametesDiploid germ cells in the ovaries and testes go through meiosis. Each gamete gets one chromosome of every pair, so it is haploid and carries A or a, never both. The amount of hereditary material is halved.
FERTILIZATIONTwo gametes make a zygoteA haploid egg and a haploid sperm fuse: n + n = 2n. The zygote is diploid again, with one set from each parent. The normal amount of hereditary material is restored.
MITOSISThe zygote builds a bodyThe zygote divides by mitosis into every cell of the body, somatic cells and germ cells alike. All are diploid with the same DNA as the zygote (A and a).
TAP A STEPFollow A and aOne pair of chromosomes: pink from the mother (A), blue from the father (a). Tap each step to see which cells have which.
06 / 41 · MODULE 3.2 · PART 1 · THE WORDS

Homologs, chromatids and ploidy

Before following chromosomes through meiosis, get the words straight. Meiosis only works in a cell that has homologous pairs: two of each kind of chromosome, one from each parent.3

Tap the buttons, or Next, to click through all 6
BEFORE SUnreplicated chromosomesEach chromosome is one DNA molecule. The pink one came from the mother and carries allele A; the blue one came from the father and carries a.
AFTER SA replicated chromosomeDNA replication happens before meiosis starts, in S phase. Each chromosome becomes two sister chromatids, identical copies with the same allele (A and A).
NON-SISTER CHROMATIDSOne chromatid from each homologA pink chromatid and a blue chromatid are non-sister chromatids: same genes in the same order, but not identical. Crossing over happens between them.
HOMOLOGOUS CHROMOSOMESThe pairSimilar in size, shape and gene content, with the same genes at the same loci, one inherited from each parent. B and b, or A and a, are different alleles of the same gene.
TETRAD (BIVALENT)The pair joined togetherIn meiosis I the two replicated homologs pair up and lie side by side: four chromatids, a tetrad or bivalent. This is the only time homologs pair.
CENTROMERECount theseOne centromere per chromosome, replicated or not. Count centromeres to count chromosomes; count chromatids to count DNA molecules.

TERMWHAT IT MEANSEXAMPLE

Sister chromatidsThe two copies in a replicated chromosomeA and A
Homologous chromosomesSimilar in size, shape and gene content; one from each parentYour chromosome 22 from your mother and your chromosome 22 from your father

TetradHomologous replicated chromosomes joined togetherA bivalent in prophase I

08 / 41 · PART 1 · LOCK IT IN

Lock it in · Part 1

  1. Asexual reproduction: one parent, identical offspring, fast growth, low variation. Sexual: two parents, mixed offspring, costly, high variation.
  2. Meiosis happens only in diploid germ cells; it makes 4 haploid gametes. Fertilization (n + n) restores 2n. Mitosis builds the body from the zygote.
  3. Somatic and germ cells are 2n with the same DNA; gametes are n with one allele of each gene.
  4. Sister chromatids = copies of one chromosome. Homologs = a pair, one from each parent, same genes at the same loci. A tetrad (bivalent) = the replicated pair joined in meiosis I.
  5. Meiosis needs homologous pairs to separate, so only a cell with at least two sets can do it.
09 / 41 · MODULE 3.2 · PART 2 · THE QUESTION

Meiosis, step by step

How does one diploid germ cell end up as four haploid gametes, with only one round of DNA replication?

10 / 41 · MODULE 3.2 · PART 2 · SAME NAMES, TWICE

Phases of meiosis: the same four as mitosis, run twice

If meiosis looks a lot like mitosis, that is because it uses the same phases: prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase. Mitosis goes through them once. Meiosis goes through them twice, meiosis I and then meiosis II, after a single round of DNA replication.1,2

Tap a button to explore
SAME NAMESProphase, metaphase, anaphase, telophaseBoth divisions use the same four phases, with the same basic jobs: condense and build a spindle, line up in the middle, pull apart, then split into two cells.Mitosis runs through them once. Meiosis runs through them twice, so each phase name gets a I or a II. Both start after one interphase, where the DNA is copied once.
MEIOSIS I VS. MITOSISSame phases, different partnersThis is where meiosis is new. In prophase I the homologs pair up and cross over, which never happens in mitosis. In metaphase I they line up in pairs, not single file. In anaphase I the homologs separate while the sister chromatids stay together.Result: 2 haploid cells (n), each chromosome still two sister chromatids.
MEIOSIS II VS. MITOSISMitosis again, with half the chromosomesMeiosis II follows straight on, with no S phase first. Each phase works just like mitosis: line up single file, then the sister chromatids separate.The difference is the starting cell: it is haploid, so the result is 4 haploid cells in all, and crossing over made every one different.
TAP ONERead across a rowEach row is one phase. Tap meiosis I or meiosis II to compare it with mitosis.
11 / 41 · MODULE 3.2 · PART 2 · THE WHOLE PROCESS

Meiosis, stage by stage

One diploid germ cell, one pair of chromosomes (2n = 2), all the way to four gametes. Watch the counts at the bottom: one round of DNA replication, then two divisions.1,2

Tap the buttons, or Next, to click through all 9
BEFORE MEIOSIS · G1A diploid germ cellOne homologous pair: pink from the mother with allele A, blue from the father with allele a. Each chromosome is one DNA molecule.
BEFORE MEIOSIS · S PHASEDNA replication, onceEvery chromosome is copied into two sister chromatids. This is the only round of DNA replication: there is none between meiosis I and II.
MEIOSIS I · PROPHASE IHomologs pair up and cross overChromosomes condense. The two homologs find each other and lie side by side (synapsis), forming a bivalent (tetrad). This is the only time homologous chromosomes pair.Non-sister chromatids exchange segments at a chiasma (crossing over): here the inner chromatids swap their tips. The nuclear envelope breaks down and the spindle forms.
MEIOSIS I · METAPHASE IPairs line up togetherEach bivalent lines up across the middle, its two homologs facing opposite poles. Spindle fibers from one pole attach to one whole homolog.
MEIOSIS I · ANAPHASE IHomologs separateThe homologs are pulled to opposite poles. The centromeres do not split: sister chromatids stay together. This is what halves the chromosome number.
MEIOSIS I · TELOPHASE ITwo haploid cellsCytokinesis gives two cells, each with one replicated chromosome: haploid (n = 1), even though each chromosome still has 2 DNA molecules. One cell got the A homolog, the other the a homolog.
MEIOSIS II · METAPHASE IILine up one by oneIn each cell the replicated chromosome lines up on its own, as in mitosis. Fibers from both poles attach to its two sister chromatids.
MEIOSIS II · ANAPHASE IISister chromatids separateThe centromeres split and the sister chromatids are pulled apart. Each chromatid is now a chromosome.
MEIOSIS II · TELOPHASE IIFour haploid gametesFour haploid cells, each with one chromosome and one DNA molecule. Two carry A and two carry a, and because of crossing over no two are identical.
12 / 41 · MODULE 3.2 · PART 2 · PROPHASE I UP CLOSE

Synapsis, bivalents and chiasmata: prophase I as it really looks

Most diagrams start prophase I with neat X-shaped pairs. Real prophase I starts as a tangle: the chromosomes "first appear as long, thin threads present throughout the nucleus," and the homologs find each other and pair up while they're still long. The tidy shapes only appear at the end.1,2

Tap the buttons, or Next, to click through all 5
EARLY PROPHASE ILong, thin, tangled threadsThe chromosomes start to condense and become visible as long, thin threads all through the nucleus, tangled together. DNA was already copied in S phase, so each thread is two sister chromatids (the two thin lines of one color).The threads are chromatin: DNA wound on proteins, not loose DNA.
SYNAPSISEach chromosome finds its homologEach chromosome pairs with its homolog, the same chromosome from the other parent, and the two zip together along their whole length, still long and wavy. This pairing is synapsis, and it happens only in meiosis.The zipped pair is a bivalent (tetrad): 2 chromosomes, 4 chromatids. Even X and Y pair, but only at their tips.
CROSSING OVERSwapping pieces while zippedWhile the homologs are zipped, two non-sister chromatids (one pink, one blue) break at the same place and rejoin to each other's piece: crossing over. Matching segments are exchanged; usually no DNA is gained or lost.Only 2 of the 4 chromatids swap at each crossover. The spots stay visible as chiasmata (✕). Where they fall is essentially random; most bivalents get at least one (humans: about 50 to 60 per meiosis).
LATE PROPHASE INow it looks like the drawingsThe threads coil up short and thick, and the bivalents finally look like the familiar tidy pictures. The chiasmata hold each pair together until anaphase I.Still count centromeres. 2 bivalents = 4 centromeres = 4 chromosomes, and 8 chromatids. Crossing over moved DNA between chromatids but didn't change any count.
METAPHASE ITop or bottom is randomThe bivalents line up across the middle, one homolog facing each pole. Which one faces up is random, and each pair lines up independently of every other pair.That's independent assortment, the reason behind Mendel's law of independent assortment (Module 3.3).

Ploidy and counts, before, during and after

The same counting rules as mitosis: chromosomes = centromeres, DNA molecules = chromatids. What changes in meiosis is the ploidy.

Meiosis vs. mitosis

Meiosis II looks like mitosis. The big differences are all in meiosis I: homologs pair, cross over and separate.1

Tap a button to explore
MITOSISSingle file, each pole grabs a sisterIn a diploid cell, each replicated chromosome lines up on its own. Homologs ignore each other.Fibers from both poles attach to every chromosome, one to each sister chromatid. So in anaphase the sisters separate.
MEIOSIS IIn pairs, each pole grabs a whole homologHomologs line up as a pair, side by side across the middle.All the fibers from one pole attach to one homolog (both its sisters), and the other pole takes the other homolog. So in anaphase I the homologs separate while the sisters stay together.

Same meiosis, different cytoplasm

Meiosis shares out the chromosomes the same way in both sexes, but in animals the cytoplasm divides very differently.1

Tap a button to explore
FEMALE1 egg and 3 polar bodiesBoth meiotic divisions split the cytoplasm very unequally. One cell keeps nearly all of it and becomes the large egg; the other three, the polar bodies, get very little and do not become eggs.
MALE4 spermThe cytoplasm divides about equally, and all four cells become sperm. While a sperm develops it loses most of its cytoplasm: little more than a nucleus in a head, with a flagellum to swim.
TAP ONEFour haploid cells either wayIn both sexes meiosis makes four haploid cells. Tap to see what becomes of them.
17 / 41 · PART 2 · LOCK IT IN

Lock it in · Part 2

  1. Meiosis uses the same four phases as mitosis (prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase), run twice: meiosis I, then meiosis II.
  2. One DNA replication (S phase), then two divisions. No replication between meiosis I and II.
  3. Meiosis I: prophase I (homologs pair into bivalents, crossing over), metaphase I (pairs line up), anaphase I (homologs separate). 2n → n.
  4. Meiosis II: metaphase II (line up one by one), anaphase II (sister chromatids separate). n → n, like mitosis.
  5. Result: 4 haploid gametes, genetically different. Human: 46 → 23 chromosomes per gamete.
  6. Sister chromatids are present at metaphase I and II; homologs are together only at metaphase I.
  7. Females: 1 egg + 3 polar bodies (unequal cytoplasm). Males: 4 sperm.
18 / 41 · MODULE 3.2 · PART 3 · THE QUESTION

Where genetic variation comes from

Two siblings get their chromosomes from the same two parents. Why aren't they identical?

19 / 41 · MODULE 3.2 · PART 3 · WHY IT MATTERS

Three ways meiosis and fertilization make variation

Genetic variation, the genetic differences among individuals in a population, is critical to a species' long-term survival: a species can only adapt to new or changing environments if it has variation. Darwin saw it in 1859: individual differences are what natural selection works on.1,2

20 / 41 · MODULE 3.2 · PART 3 · VARIATION #1

Crossing over and recombination

Crossing over happens in prophase I, while the homologs are paired as a bivalent. Usually 1 to 3 chiasmata form per chromosome.3,2

Tap the buttons, or Next, to click through all 4
PROPHASE IThe homologs pair upThe mother's chromosome carries A and D; the father's carries a and d. Each is two sister chromatids.
A CHIASMA FORMSNon-sister chromatids crossTwo non-sister chromatids, one pink and one blue, break at the same place. The chiasma also holds the homologs together until anaphase I.
THEY SWAPMatching segments are exchangedThe broken ends rejoin the other chromatid. The exchange is precise: the same genes, in the same order, no DNA gained or lost. Only the alleles below the break are swapped.
THE RESULTRecombinant chromatidsTwo chromatids keep the parental combinations (A D and a d). Two are recombinant (A d and a D): combinations that neither parent's chromosome had. Each goes to a different gamete.
21 / 41 · MODULE 3.2 · PART 3 · VARIATION #2

Independent assortment

At metaphase I, each pair lines up on its own, maternal homolog facing one pole or the other at random. With n pairs there are 2ⁿ combinations. One human can make gametes with 2²³, about 8 million, different combinations of chromosomes.3,2

Tap a button to explore
WAY 1Both maternal homologs face one polePink A and pink B go one way, blue a and blue b the other. Gametes: AB and ab.
WAY 2The short pair is flippedPink A goes with blue b, blue a with pink B. Gametes: Ab and aB.
ALL FOUR2² = 4 kinds of gameteTwo pairs, each with 2 orientations: 2 × 2 = 4 combinations. Each orientation is equally likely in every germ cell.
TAP ONEWhat assorts independently?The homologous pairs: how one pair lines up has no effect on how the other lines up.
22 / 41 · MODULE 3.2 · PART 3 · VARIATION #3

Random fertilization

Any of a mother's eggs can meet any of a father's sperm. For humans, one couple can make 2²³ × 2²³, about 70 trillion, unique zygotes, and that is without the extra variety from crossing over.2

23 / 41 · PART 3 · LOCK IT IN

Lock it in · Part 3

  1. Genetic variation lets a species adapt; sexual reproduction increases it in three places.
  2. Crossing over (prophase I): non-sister chromatids exchange segments at chiasmata, making recombinant chromosomes.
  3. Independent assortment (metaphase I): pairs orient at random, 2ⁿ combinations; 2²³ ≈ 8 million in humans.
  4. Random fertilization: 2ⁿ × 2ⁿ, about 70 trillion zygotes per human couple.
  5. All three only shuffle existing alleles. New alleles come from mutation.
24 / 41 · MODULE 3.2 · PART 4 · THE QUESTION

Point mutations

Every allele began as a mutation. What kinds of small changes can happen to DNA, and what do they do to a protein?

25 / 41 · MODULE 3.2 · PART 4 · START HERE

What is a mutation?

A mutation is any heritable change in the genetic material: it is stable and is passed on through cell division (meiosis, mitosis or binary fission). Mutation is the ultimate source of genetic variation: every allele began as one.1,2

Tap a button to explore
NEUTRALNo effect on fitnessMost mutations in noncoding DNA are neutral, and so are synonymous mutations. Neutral is the most common kind.
DELETERIOUSLowers fitnessMost missense, nonsense and frameshift mutations are deleterious: they change or break a protein.
BENEFICIALRaises fitnessFew mutations, coding or noncoding, are beneficial (advantageous). Example: mutations in an enhancer that keep the lactase gene on in adults, so they can digest milk.
TAP ONEThree possible effectsWhether a mutation helps or harms depends on where it lands, and on the environment.
26 / 41 · MODULE 3.2 · PART 4 · HOW IT HAPPENS

How a copying error becomes a mutation, and how often

Most mistakes in DNA replication are fixed right away: DNA polymerase proofreads, and repair enzymes catch most of the rest. A fixed mistake is not a mutation. A mutation is a mistake that escapes repair and is then copied.1

Tap the buttons, or Next, to click through all 4
THE ORIGINALA T-A base pairA matches T and G matches C. Watch the highlighted T-A pair.
THE MISTAKEA G across from the TDuring replication, DNA polymerase puts a G across from the T. If proofreading and repair miss it, the new DNA has a T-G mismatch.
THE NEXT REPLICATIONEach strand becomes a templateThe T strand is copied into a normal T-A pair. The G strand is copied into a C-G pair.
PERMANENTA substitutionThe C-G pair is perfectly matched, so nothing looks wrong and it is copied faithfully from then on: T-A has been replaced by C-G, a substitution, a point mutation. A variant like this that becomes common in a population is a single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP).
27 / 41 · MODULE 3.2 · PART 4 · SUBSTITUTIONS

One letter swapped: synonymous, missense, nonsense

A substitution replaces one nucleotide with another. In a coding region, what it does depends on how the mRNA codon changes. 64 codons code for 20 amino acids and 3 stops, so most amino acids have several codons (you don't need to memorize the code).3,1,2

Tap the buttons, or Next, to click through all 4
THE ORIGINALTTA → UUA → leucineThe coding strand reads TTA, the template strand AAT, so the mRNA codon is UUA, which codes for leucine.
MISSENSE (NONSYNONYMOUS)UUA → GUA: valineA different amino acid. Missense and nonsynonymous mean the same thing. The protein may work worse, or not at all, depending on the change. (The sickle-cell allele is a missense mutation: glutamic acid to valine.)
NONSENSEUUA → UAA: STOPAn early stop codon: translation ends early and the protein is cut short, so it is nearly always nonfunctional. A nonsense mutation is not counted as missense or nonsynonymous.
SYNONYMOUSUUA → CUA: still leucineThe same amino acid, so the protein does not change and the phenotype does not change. Synonymous codons usually differ at the third position, though here it is the first. The textbook's example is in beta-globin: GAG → GAA, both glutamic acid.
28 / 41 · MODULE 3.2 · PART 4 · INDELS

Letters added or lost: indels and frameshifts

An indel is an insertion or deletion of one or more base pairs. The name covers both because, comparing two sequences, a gap in one could be an insertion in the other or a deletion in the first. Unlike a substitution, an indel changes the length of the DNA.3,1,2

Tap the buttons, or Next, to click through all 4
THE READING FRAMEThree letters at a timeA ribosome reads mRNA in codons of three, starting from the start codon, just as you read this sentence in three-letter words.
INSERT 1 · FRAMESHIFTEverything after it changesOne extra letter shifts the frame: every word after it is gibberish. In DNA, every codon downstream codes for a different amino acid, often hitting an early stop.
DELETE 1 · FRAMESHIFTSame problemLosing one letter (or 2, 4, 5...) shifts the frame the other way. Any indel that is not a multiple of 3 is a frameshift.
INSERT 3 · IN FRAMEOne extra wordThree letters add exactly one codon: one extra amino acid (or one fewer for a deletion), and the rest of the protein is unchanged.
29 / 41 · MODULE 3.2 · PART 4 · CODING VS. NONCODING

Which types need a coding region?

Most of the human genome does not code for protein: about 2.5% does, and more than 90% of the nucleotides seem free to vary without harm. That is why each of us can carry about 60 new mutations and be fine. A mutation in noncoding DNA usually has no effect, but some noncoding DNA regulates genes, and a mutation there can matter.1,3

30 / 41 · MODULE 3.2 · PART 4 · GENOTYPE TO PHENOTYPE

From a change in DNA to a change in the organism

Genetic variation matters for evolution because it creates heritable differences in phenotype. But many mutations change no trait at all, and the ones that do can have different effects depending on the rest of the genotype and on the environment.1,2

Tap a button to explore
ALLELE AThe most commonGAG codes for glutamic acid. People with two copies (homozygous AA) have typical hemoglobin.
ALLELE SOne base changed: a missense mutationGTG codes for valine. One amino acid changes the way the protein folds and works: SS causes sickle-cell anemia. AS (heterozygous) gives only a mild anemia, and where malaria is common it protects against malaria, so there it is beneficial. Where there is no malaria, it is harmful.
ALLELE CAnother missense mutationAAG codes for lysine. AC gives partial protection against malaria; CC gives more protection and only a very mild anemia.
TAP AN ALLELEHow a DNA change reaches the phenotypeDNA sequence → mRNA codon → amino acid sequence → how the protein folds → how it works → the trait. You don't need to memorize these alleles: they show the principle.
31 / 41 · PART 4 · LOCK IT IN

Lock it in · Part 4

  1. A mutation is a heritable change in DNA, the ultimate source of genetic variation. It happens by chance, mostly during DNA replication.
  2. Most mutations are neutral; most missense, nonsense and frameshift mutations are deleterious; a few are beneficial.
  3. Substitution (one base swapped): synonymous (same amino acid), missense = nonsynonymous (different amino acid), nonsense (early stop).
  4. Indel (bases added or lost): not a multiple of 3 = frameshift; a multiple of 3 adds or removes whole amino acids.
  5. Synonymous, missense, nonsense and frameshift happen only in coding regions; substitutions and indels can happen anywhere.
  6. A mismatch that escapes repair becomes permanent at the next replication. Mutations are rare per nucleotide but common per genome; most new ones come from the father.
  7. Genotype + environment → phenotype. Alleles are different DNA sequences (polymorphisms). Effects can depend on homozygous vs. heterozygous and on the environment.
32 / 41 · MODULE 3.2 · PART 5 · THE QUESTION

Chromosomal mutations, and where mutations come from

What happens when whole chunks of chromosomes, or whole chromosomes, go wrong, and do mutations happen because an organism needs them?

33 / 41 · MODULE 3.2 · PART 5 · BIG CHANGES

Chromosomal mutations

Some mutations affect large regions: hundreds of thousands to millions of nucleotides, often big enough to see under a microscope. They change how many copies of genes there are, or where the genes sit.1,2

Tap the buttons, or Next, to click through all 4
GENE DUPLICATIONAn extra copyA segment appears twice. A duplicated gene's extra copy is free to collect mutations, and it often ends up coding for a protein with a new function. That is how gene families arise.
GENE DELETIONA missing pieceA chromosome loses a segment and the genes in it. Usually more harmful than a duplication of the same region.
INVERSIONFlipped aroundBoth DNA strands break in two places and the piece reattaches in reverse orientation, changing the order of genes. If whole genes and their regulatory sequences survive the breaks, it may have no effect.
RECIPROCAL TRANSLOCATIONTwo chromosomes swapTwo non-homologous chromosomes break (both strands), and each broken piece attaches to the other chromosome. It may or may not have effects, depending on where the breaks are and whether regulatory regions are hit.
34 / 41 · MODULE 3.2 · PART 5 · WRONG NUMBERS

Nondisjunction: extra or missing chromosomes

Nondisjunction is the failure of homologs or sister chromatids to separate. It can happen in mitosis, meiosis I or meiosis II. In meiosis it gives gametes with an extra or missing chromosome, and the zygote they make is aneuploid.3,2,4

Tap the buttons, or Next, to click through all 4
NORMAL MEIOSISEvery sperm has 23X and Y are a pair: they separate in meiosis I. Sister chromatids separate in meiosis II. Every sperm gets one chromosome 22 and either an X or a Y.
MEIOSIS I NONDISJUNCTIONHomologs fail to separateX and Y go to the same pole. All four sperm are abnormal: two with X, Y and 22 (24 chromosomes in humans) and two with no sex chromosome (22).
MEIOSIS II NONDISJUNCTIONSister chromatids fail to separateMeiosis I was normal, but in one cell the Y's sister chromatids stay together. Two sperm are normal, one has two Y's (24) and one has none (22).
FERTILIZATIONAn aneuploid zygoteA sperm with X and Y + a normal egg (X) = 47, XXY: one extra chromosome (Klinefelter syndrome). A sperm with no sex chromosome + an egg = 45, X: one missing (Turner syndrome).
35 / 41 · MODULE 3.2 · PART 5 · READ IT

Reading a karyotype

A karyotype shows a cell's condensed chromosomes, sorted into pairs from the longest to the shortest, with the sex chromosomes last. It is how extra or missing chromosomes are found.3

Tap the buttons, or Next, to click through all 3
A TYPICAL MALE46, XY22 numbered pairs plus X and Y: 46 chromosomes, diploid. (A typical female is 46, XX.)
TRISOMY 2147, +21Three copies of chromosome 21: Down syndrome. It comes from nondisjunction of chromosome 21 in a parent's meiosis.
AN EXTRA X47, XXYTwo X chromosomes and a Y: Klinefelter syndrome, the result drawn in the section above.
36 / 41 · MODULE 3.2 · PART 5 · HOW DO WE KNOW?

Mutations are random: the Lederbergs' experiment

Treat bacteria with an antibiotic and the survivors are resistant. Did the antibiotic cause resistance mutations, or were resistant cells already there? Esther and Joshua Lederberg tested it in 1952 with replica plating.5,6,4

Tap the buttons, or Next, to click through all 4
SETUPCopy the coloniesBacteria grow on a master plate with no antibiotic; each colony is thousands of identical cells from a single cell. A sterile velvet disk picks up cells from every colony and stamps them, in the same positions, onto a fresh plate that contains antibiotic (the selective plate). A copy stamped onto a plate without antibiotic is the control: every colony grows there.
RESULT 1Only two colonies growOn the antibiotic plate, only the colonies at two spots (X and Y) grow. The rest die.
GO BACKFind the same spots on the originalBecause the stamp kept positions, the Lederbergs could find the colonies at X and Y on the original plate, which had never touched antibiotic.
RESULT 2They were already resistantFrom those original colonies the Lederbergs grew a pure culture of antibiotic-resistant bacteria, although those cells had never met the antibiotic. The resistance mutations existed before exposure. The antibiotic did not cause them: it selected them.
37 / 41 · MODULE 3.2 · PART 5 · WHO INHERITS IT

Germ-line vs. somatic mutations

A mutation can happen in any cell, but only those in germ cells can reach the next generation.6,4

Tap a button to explore
SOMATIC MUTATIONStays in the bodyA mutation in a body cell is passed to that cell's descendants by mitosis (a patch of skin, a sectored flower, sometimes a cancer), but not to offspring, because gametes don't come from that cell.
GERM-LINE MUTATIONPassed to offspringA mutation in a germ cell can end up in a gamete. A child who grows from that gamete has the mutation in every cell, including its own germ cells, so it can be passed on again.
TAP ONEWhere did it happen?Tap a somatic mutation, then a germ-line mutation.
38 / 41 · MODULE 3.2 · PART 5 · PUT IT TOGETHER

Important ideas about mutations

Genotype is an organism's genetic makeup; phenotype is its observable traits. Different alleles are different DNA sequences, and mutations make them. Whether a mutation changes the phenotype depends on how it affects gene function, and often on the environment.6,4

39 / 41 · MODULE 3.2 · PART 5 · SORT THEM

Every mutation type, sorted

Four questions from class: which types can be point mutations, which must be in coding regions, which can be in noncoding regions, and which are chromosomal?2,4

40 / 41 · PART 5 · LOCK IT IN

Lock it in · Part 5

  1. Chromosomal mutations: gene duplication (extra copy, can gain a new function), gene deletion, inversion (order reversed), reciprocal translocation (non-homologous chromosomes swap pieces).
  2. Nondisjunction (homologs in meiosis I, or sisters in meiosis II, fail to separate) gives gametes with n + 1 or n − 1; the zygote is aneuploid (47, XXY; 47, +21; 45, X). A whole set → polyploidy.
  3. A karyotype shows number, pairs, sex chromosomes and large changes, not point mutations.
  4. The Lederbergs' replica plating: resistant colonies existed before the antibiotic. Mutations are random; the environment selects.
  5. Only germ-line mutations are passed to offspring; somatic ones stay in the body.
  6. Most mutations are neutral; a noncoding mutation can be beneficial by changing gene regulation (lactase persistence).
